notes.explains: With all four knights developed, White strikes with d4, hitting the e5-pawn and prying the center open before Black finishes coordinating.
notes.teaches: The Scotch Four Knights breaks the center early to cash in a lead in development.

notes.explains: The pawn to c4 braces the advanced d5-wedge and stakes out queenside space, hinting at a future c5 break.
notes.teaches: Support an advanced pawn wedge and expand behind it before committing to action.

notes.explains: King to h2 is quietly prophylactic — it steps off the checking diagonals and clears the way for a kingside pawn storm with g3 and f4.
notes.teaches: Tuck the king to safety before launching a pawn advance in front of it.

notes.explains: Bishop to c4 is the gambit's soul — instead of hurrying to win back the d4-pawn, White throws the bishop onto the a2-g8 diagonal, aiming at f7 with fast Italian-style development.
notes.teaches: In a gambit, prize rapid piece activity and pressure over recovering the pawn.

notes.explains: Now d4 lands with real bite — it threatens a fork with d5 and forces Black to release the central tension on White's terms.
notes.teaches: Time the central break so it carries a concrete threat, forcing the exchanges you want.

notes.explains: f4 grabs kingside space and begins to entomb the bishop on e6 — with f5 coming, that piece is running out of safe squares.
notes.teaches: Expand with pawns to trap a poorly-placed enemy bishop.

notes.explains: With the bishop pair traded off and e5 no longer the plan, Black changes gears with c5, carving open the long diagonal for the fianchettoed bishop on g7 and steering into a Benoni structure.
notes.teaches: When the fianchettoed bishop is your main asset, open its long diagonal with a timely c5.
notes.plans: Benoni queenside play with a6 and b5.

notes.explains: The pawn to b5 launches the Benoni's signature queenside expansion, prising open lines where Black is strongest while the bishop on e5 rakes the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: In the Benoni, roll out b5 to open the queenside where you hold the pawn majority.

notes.explains: Black turns the queen trade into a weapon: with the queens gone, the advancing c-pawn and the long-diagonal bishop combine, and the bishop snaps the rook off a1 to win the exchange and the game.
notes.teaches: A queen trade isn't always drawish — here it strips the defence so the long-diagonal bishop wins material.

notes.explains: After the knight to c3 the Open Sicilian reaches its great fork: the fianchetto to g6 is the Dragon, the knight to c6 is the Classical, and the little pawn to a6 is the Najdorf — each a different world.
notes.teaches: The 5th-move choice defines your whole Sicilian — Dragon, Classical, or Najdorf.
notes.plans: Pick the Najdorf: maximum flexibility.

notes.explains: The pawn to a6 is the Najdorf — the most respected Sicilian of all. It takes the b5-square away from White's pieces and keeps every plan open, deciding on the setup only after White commits.
notes.teaches: …a6 is prophylaxis plus flexibility — it denies b5 and delays Black's commitment.
notes.plans: Wait for White's system, then choose …e5 or …e6 accordingly.

notes.explains: Bishop to c5 chooses the Giuoco Piano — a calm, principled setup that sidesteps the sharp Two Knights lines and is far easier to steer at speed.
notes.teaches: Mirror the opponent's active bishop and develop soundly rather than inviting forcing theory.

notes.explains: The bishop checks from b4 before recapturing — this is the whole point. It forces White to block, and only then does Black strike back at the big center.
notes.teaches: Insert a forcing check to win a tempo before resolving the central tension.

notes.explains: With an extra pawn banked, d5 hits the bishop and frees Black's game; the light bishop will settle on e6, guarding d5 and f7 at once.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, open lines for your pieces and simplify toward the win.

notes.explains: Queen to f6 is the main move — it heaps pressure on the knight on d4 and steps out of the Nxc6-then-Bxc5 fork that White was about to spring.
notes.teaches: In the Scotch, meet the d4-knight with piece pressure while dodging the c6/c5 fork trick.

notes.explains: White grabs the pawn on e5, a knowingly unsound piece sacrifice — the whole idea is a fast attack on f7 and the uncastled king, betting the opponent can't defend cleanly.
notes.teaches: A speculative sac trades material for initiative against a king stuck in the center — an attacking try, not a sound line.

notes.explains: Down a piece, White plays d3 to open the light bishop's diagonal and rush development — with the sac made, only quick, purposeful moves can justify it.
notes.teaches: After a sacrifice every move must develop with threats; slow play refutes it.

notes.explains: f4 tears open the f-file toward Black's king — the point of the sacrifice, manufacturing concrete kingside pressure before the extra piece can speak.
notes.teaches: Convert a material investment into an open file and direct attacking chances.

notes.explains: The Alekhine: Black offers the knight as a target, daring White's pawns forward. The whole opening is a provocation — let the centre advance, then strike at it.
notes.teaches: The Alekhine is hypermodern — invite the pawn centre, then undermine it.
notes.plans: Build the big centre, but be ready to defend it.

notes.explains: The pawn to f4 completes the Four Pawns Attack — pawns on c4, d4, e4 and f4, absolute central domination. It is the most ambitious try, but it comes at the cost of development: play it carelessly and White can be crushed inside five moves.
notes.teaches: Maximum space and lagging development are two sides of one coin — the Four Pawns must be handled precisely.
notes.plans: Hold the centre together and catch up in development.

notes.explains: The key restraint: do NOT push c5 to gain a tempo — that would concede the d5-square as a permanent outpost and tear a hole in the centre. Instead defend the e-pawn by developing the bishop to e3, keeping the whole pawn mass intact.
notes.teaches: Don't chase a tempo with a pawn push that hands the opponent a permanent hole — develop to defend instead.
notes.plans: Hold d5 under control; develop the pieces behind the centre.

notes.explains: Develop the knight to c3. It supports the centre and readies the answer to the knight jump to b4 — the rook simply steps to c1 and the intruder achieves nothing.
notes.teaches: Develop toward your weaknesses — the c3-knight and c1-rook cover the b4 and c-file ideas.
notes.plans: Complete development, then expand.

notes.explains: Now the knight comes to f3. With enough pieces out, the pin by the bishop on g4 has lost its sting, so it is time to finish developing and think about castling.
notes.teaches: A pin is only dangerous while you're underdeveloped — once you can meet it, ignore it and develop.
notes.plans: Castle and turn to the attack.

notes.explains: Once Black has castled queenside, the pawn to c5 changes everything: it clamps the position and jump-starts a queenside pawn-storm straight at the black king, with the queen ready to swing out to a4 and join in.
notes.teaches: Against a queenside-castled king, a pawn clamp like c5 is the first move of a direct attack.
notes.plans: Push the queenside pawns and bring the queen to a4.

notes.explains: The pawn to d4 is the Alapin's whole idea — build the classical centre. After the exchange, White recaptures with a pawn and stands on a broad, mobile centre.
notes.teaches: c3 supports d4 — the point of the Alapin is the pawn centre.
notes.plans: Occupy the centre and develop naturally.

notes.explains: Develop the knight to c3, adding a piece to the centre. When Black pins with the bishop on b4, the bishop to g5 is a natural follow-up, creating pressure of its own.
notes.teaches: Develop toward the centre; meet a pin with counter-development, not passive defence.
notes.plans: Complete development and keep the central pull.

notes.explains: The fianchetto with g3 — an effective, low-theory system against the Qa5 Scandinavian that many opponents in this range have never faced.
notes.teaches: A quiet fianchetto is a practical surprise weapon precisely because it's under-prepared.
notes.plans: Fianchetto, develop with Nge2, and build the plan.

notes.explains: The knight goes to e2, not f3 — putting it on f3 would block the very bishop we fianchettoed. Keeping the long diagonal open is the whole idea.
notes.teaches: Route the knight to e2 so the fianchettoed bishop breathes.
notes.plans: Complete development, then advance the queenside.

notes.explains: The pawn to h3 is a no-brainer to throw in: it questions the bishop on g4 and, crucially, opens the possibility of a later g4 to harass it further — a free improving move.
notes.teaches: A prophylactic h3 that also unlocks g4 is a useful, low-commitment gain.
notes.plans: Follow with development and the queenside break.

notes.explains: The pawn to d3 completes the setup — it opens the fianchettoed bishop's diagonal and readies the main plan. With everything harmonious, White can turn to the queenside.
notes.teaches: Open your key bishop's diagonal as you finish developing.
notes.plans: Then execute the queenside expansion.

notes.explains: The pawn to f3 is the Sämisch — White braces e4 and prepares to castle long and storm the kingside with g4 and the h-pawn. It also denies Black's knight the g4 square.
notes.teaches: The Sämisch pairs a big centre with a pawn-storm attack; f3 is its keystone.
notes.plans: Be3, Qd2, castle long, then push g4 and h4.

notes.explains: Black's b5 lunges on the queenside where White's king sits, but it's premature. White cracks the position open first with the capture on c6, exposing the weak d6-pawn and clearing lines to it.
notes.teaches: Meet a flank pawn-lunge by opening the centre before it gathers momentum.

notes.explains: The pressure converges: several pieces bear down on d6 and the queen simply collects it. Black's loose queenside play has left him a pawn down and clearly worse.
notes.teaches: When several attackers hit one weak pawn, it falls — punish over-extension concretely.

notes.explains: d4 is the principled reply to the Philidor — Black's d6 blocks his own bishop and develops nothing, so opening the center punishes both concessions at once.
notes.teaches: Open the center against a defense that develops slowly and hems in its own pieces.

notes.explains: The knight leaps to the d5 outpost — a dream square, protected and unassailable, dominating the center and eyeing weaknesses around Black's king.
notes.teaches: Plant a knight on a central outpost the opponent can't chase, and let it dominate.

notes.explains: The bishop completes its maneuver to c3, seizing the long dark diagonal that points straight at g7 and Black's king.
notes.teaches: Reroute a bishop onto the long diagonal to team up with an outpost knight against the castled king.

notes.explains: The bishop check on b5 — an easy-to-play line that dodges heavy theory. It forces a piece to appear on d7, an awkward square for Black.
notes.teaches: The b5 check trades a little material tension for an easy, slightly better game.
notes.plans: Return the pawn later, keep the space and the better bishop.

notes.explains: When Black strikes with c5, the clamp is the pawn to c4 followed by d5 — driving a pawn deep and establishing a firm central presence Black must play around.
notes.teaches: Answer a wing break by clamping the centre with c4 and d5.
notes.plans: Fix the centre, then finish development.

notes.explains: With the pawn wedged on d5 and Black committed to e6, White has a pleasant space advantage and a clear plan — a comfortable, low-risk edge out of the opening.
notes.teaches: A protected pawn on d5 cramping the opponent is a durable, easy-to-play plus.
notes.plans: Develop behind the clamp and press.

notes.explains: The bishop check on b5 — an easy-to-learn, effective line against the Nf6 Scandinavian. It forces Black to block and commit awkwardly.
notes.teaches: The b5 check is a low-theory way to get a pleasant, slightly better game against the Scandinavian.
notes.plans: Provoke a clumsy block, then develop with a pull.

notes.explains: Most players block with the bishop to d7 — but that piece is poorly placed: it deprives the queen's knight of its natural d7-square and clogs Black's development.
notes.teaches: A blocking bishop on d7 is a liability — it robs the b8-knight of its best square.
notes.plans: Keep that bishop stuck; don't trade it off.

notes.explains: Retreat the bishop to e2 rather than allowing an exchange — the whole idea is to leave Black's awkward d7-bishop on the board, a lasting inconvenience.
notes.teaches: Preserve the opponent's bad piece by declining the trade.
notes.plans: Recover the d5-pawn and take the centre.

notes.explains: Grab the centre with the pawn to d4 — and it is important to start with d4, not a sloppy e6-type move that would leave the bishop and the g2-square under fire.
notes.teaches: Move order matters — take the centre with d4 before the pieces can be harassed.
notes.plans: Complete development behind the centre.

notes.explains: Develop the knight to c6 — principled, by-the-book play. With the extra space and Black's awkward bishop, White simply stands more comfortably.
notes.teaches: When you have a structural edge, keep developing soundly — the advantage compounds.
notes.plans: Finish development and press the space.

notes.explains: Bishop to c5 hits the knight on d4 and takes aim at f2 — a slightly offbeat but sound reply to the Four Knights Scotch that many White players don't know as deeply as the main Bb4.
notes.teaches: Pick a solid sideline your opponent is less booked on to steer the game your way.

notes.explains: d6 clamps down on e5 for good, drawing the sting from any e4-e5 break and handing Black's pieces a stable base.
notes.teaches: Fix the center with a pawn to deny the opponent a freeing break.

notes.explains: g5 kicks the bishop off h4 and grabs kingside space, unveiling the plan to round up the e4-pawn — Black's king is safer than it looks.
notes.teaches: A well-timed flank pawn thrust can gain space and win a target when your king is genuinely safe.

notes.explains: White meets the King's Indian with the quiet fianchetto — the pawn to g3 and bishop to g2. It is the most positional, least forcing anti-KID setup, aiming to control the centre from a distance.
notes.teaches: The Fianchetto Variation is White's calm, positional answer to the King's Indian.
notes.plans: Set up the standard KID: d6, O-O, and a central break.

notes.explains: White's early pawn to d5 is not a principled continuation here — it is a touch premature, releasing the central tension and handing Black clear targets and a clear plan.
notes.teaches: An early d5 in the fianchetto lines can be premature, defining the centre in Black's favour.
notes.plans: Reroute the knight and strike at the pawn chain.

notes.explains: The knight reroutes to b6, eyeing the c4-pawn — and note the trap under the surface: the natural c6 here actually loses a pawn, so the knight manoeuvre is the accurate way to challenge White's centre.
notes.teaches: Reroute the knight to pressure c4 rather than the natural c6 break, which drops a pawn here.
notes.plans: Pile on c4 and open lines on the queenside.

notes.explains: The pawn to f3 is the Fantasy Variation — White keeps the big centre and plays for a rich, tactical middlegame rather than a theoretical duel.
notes.teaches: f3 defends the centre with a pawn and steers toward sharp, less-charted play.

notes.explains: The bishop to c4 trains on f7 and must stay on that diagonal — it is what keeps the pressure on f7 alive for the tactics to come.
notes.teaches: Keep the light-squared bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal; f7 is the target the whole attack leans on.
notes.plans: Castle, then build against f7.

notes.explains: The quiet pawn to c3 shores up d4, the pawn holding White's centre. If d4 ever falls, a black knight lands on the e5 outpost and White is in trouble, so the centre is secured first.
notes.teaches: Before attacking, defend the central pawn that keeps the enemy knight out of e5.

notes.explains: Rather than a caveman pawn storm, White improves the pieces: the knight to c4 eyes the bishop on d6 and the dark squares. Against opposite-side castling, a piece build-up is a valid, less committal plan.
notes.teaches: Opposite-side castling can be attacked with pieces, not only by hurling pawns.

notes.explains: The bishop to f5 comes out before e6 could ever trap it — the whole point of Black's Advance play. Unlike the French, the light-squared bishop is active, outside the pawn chain.
notes.teaches: In the Advance Caro, get the bishop to f5 before e6; that free bishop is Black's edge over the French.
notes.plans: Play e6, then hit d4 with c5 and the pieces.

notes.explains: The pawn to c5 strikes the base of White's chain at d4 — the standard method: undermine the pawn that holds the whole structure together.
notes.teaches: Attack a pawn chain at its base; here c5 goes after d4.

notes.explains: Recapturing on f5 with the knight is the subtle point — the knight now joins in, giving Black two attackers bearing down on the d4-pawn.
notes.teaches: Recapture toward the target: the knight on f5 adds pressure to d4.

notes.explains: The pressure tells: the knight snaps off d4, winning the pawn cleanly. White's overworked defenders simply can't hold the base of the chain.
notes.teaches: When enough pieces converge on a pawn chain's base, the base falls.

notes.explains: Against White's early space grab with d5, Black strikes at its base with c6. The plan is simple: undermine and trade off the overextended pawn, and the extra space evaporates.
notes.teaches: Meet a premature space grab by challenging the advanced pawn at its base.
notes.plans: Develop smoothly and exploit White's loose, overextended setup.

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to f5 with tempo, hitting White's queen on c2 and forcing a concession. Every move gains time because White's pieces are placed so awkwardly.
notes.teaches: Develop with a threat against a poorly-placed queen — each tempo compounds.

notes.explains: Black's f5 is a raw gambit that ignores development; d4 is the reflex — hit back in the center at once, where the extra tempo tells hardest.
notes.teaches: Answer a premature flank pawn thrust by striking in the center.

notes.explains: Rather than grabbing the e4-pawn — which leaves the knights loose — White takes on e5 with the knight, keeping the pieces coordinated and the center firm.
notes.teaches: When two captures are on offer, take the one that keeps your pieces coordinated, not the greedy one.

notes.explains: Bishop to b3 piles onto the d5-pawn; with Black's dark-squared bishop already traded off, those central pawns are chronic weaknesses to harvest.
notes.teaches: Aim pieces at a pawn the opponent can no longer defend after a key trade.

notes.explains: The pawn to d5 is the Elephant Gambit — a more serious try than its reputation suggests, and worth knowing how to meet precisely.
notes.teaches: Even offbeat gambits deserve a known, precise refutation rather than improvisation.
notes.plans: Take the pawn correctly and consolidate the extra material.

notes.explains: The bishop to b5 is the Rossolimo — a positional anti-Sicilian that pins toward the c6-knight. The clean, natural answer is the fianchetto with the pawn to g6.
notes.teaches: Meet the Rossolimo with …g6 for a sound, Dragon-like structure without the heavy theory.
notes.plans: Fianchetto the bishop to g7 and castle.

notes.explains: The bishop settles on g7, commanding the long diagonal. Black gets the Dragon's best piece and a solid, flexible position — none of the sharp Yugoslav-Attack danger.
notes.teaches: The g7-bishop gives Rossolimo Black the Dragon's power piece without its risks.
notes.plans: Castle, then contest the centre with …e5 or …d6/…Nf6.

notes.explains: Instead of the traditional pawn to d4, the bishop check on b5 is a sharp, well-regarded try — it develops with tempo and forces a block before White commits the centre. It does require knowing a little theory.
notes.teaches: A tempo-gaining Bb5+ can be a stronger move-order than the automatic d4.
notes.plans: Provoke the block, then choose the central setup.

notes.explains: With the pieces out, d4 cracks open the center against the cramped Philidor — Black's d6-pawn hems in his own bishop, so opening lines magnifies that lag.
notes.teaches: Open the center against a passive setup once your own pieces are ready.

notes.explains: The knight jumps to d5, offering to swap Black's fine bishop on c6 — trading a passive piece is no concession when it nets you the bishop pair in an open position.
notes.teaches: A trade that removes the opponent's best piece and hands you the bishop pair is a gain, not a concession.

notes.explains: The French, and the pawn to e5 sets up the Advance. What follows is the Nimzowitsch treatment — a dangerous line that teaches closed structures and positional chess as much as it wins games.
notes.teaches: The Nimzowitsch Advance is a positional weapon built around the e5-clamp.
notes.plans: e5, then Nf3 without c3.

notes.explains: Instead of the automatic c3 to prop up the chain, slip through the cracks with the knight to f3 — develop as if nothing were wrong and let Black ruin the pawn chain by capturing on d4. It looks utterly counter-intuitive, and that's the point.
notes.teaches: Nf3 over c3: concede the d4-pawn's shelter for rapid development.
notes.plans: Nf3, allow ...cxd4, develop fast.

notes.explains: The bishop's best square is d3, behind the pawn. The bishop to b5 is a paper tiger — Black just blocks with the bishop to d7 — whereas from d3 it eyes h7, so if Black castles kingside a Greek-gift sacrifice is always waiting.
notes.teaches: Post the bishop on d3 for the h7 diagonal and the Greek-gift, not on b5 where the pin is easily blocked.
notes.plans: Bd3, keep Bxh7+ in reserve.

notes.explains: Black lunges with the pawn to c4, and the bishop simply steps back to e2. In a closed centre you can afford to move the same piece twice — and White has provoked c4, which relieves all the pressure on d4 and hands White a free hand on the queenside.
notes.teaches: In a closed position, provoking ...c4 releases the central tension and frees you to attack a wing.
notes.plans: Be2, then break the queenside chain.

notes.explains: Now break the chain at its links: the pawn to b3 leans on c4, and the pawn to a4 will lean on b5. Classic pawn play — put pressure on both pawns at once and dismantle the structure without delay.
notes.teaches: Attack a pawn chain by pressuring its members with your own pawns, base first.
notes.plans: b3 and a4 to break c4/b5.

notes.explains: The pawn to a4 hits b5, the base of the chain — and note the tactical detail: the defence ...a6 is futile, because after the trade on b5 Black can't recapture with the a-pawn without hanging the undefended rook on a8. Timing is everything; strike before Black consolidates.
notes.teaches: a4 undermines b5; ...a6 fails because ...axb5 drops the a8-rook — act before the defender arrives.
notes.plans: a4 now, exploit the loose rook.

notes.explains: Take the base first — the capture on b5 removes the linchpin of the chain. Only then does the pawn on c4 fall, and with it comes a permanent structural weakness.
notes.teaches: Eliminate the base of a pawn chain before harvesting the pawns it supported.
notes.plans: axb5 first, then win c4.

notes.explains: After the trades resolve on c4, White has achieved exactly the plan: a long-term, permanent weakness on the queenside. The c4-pawn is a chronic target that isn't going anywhere.
notes.teaches: Convert temporary pressure into a permanent structural weakness you can besiege at leisure.
notes.plans: Fix c4, then surround it.

notes.explains: Castle first — it's safe, because Black has no way to get at the d4-pawn, and the knight on f3 guards e5 so a capture there is impossible. Then the pawn to c3 secures d4, and only after those preliminaries does White set about winning c4.
notes.teaches: Secure your own position (king safety, hold d4/e5) before going after the target.
notes.plans: O-O, c3, then win c4.

notes.explains: Black tries the pawn to f6 to open the centre — but that's counterproductive when you're behind in development, so welcome it. Capture on f6 and pry open the e-file, right onto the chronic weakness on e6.
notes.teaches: Welcome the opponent opening the centre when you're better developed — it exposes his weaknesses.
notes.plans: exf6, open the e-file onto e6.

notes.explains: No need to force it — the controlled move is the rook to e1, keeping the queen back to guard d4 for now. With two weaknesses on e6 and c4 and no time to develop, Black simply cannot hold.
notes.teaches: With two weaknesses and a lead, apply pressure calmly — the second weakness does the work.
notes.plans: Re1, pile on e6.

notes.explains: The king came out to f7 to defend e6, but the knight to g5 forks it with check and knocks it back. The pawn is won — though there's still technique to show with the king this exposed.
notes.teaches: A knight check can fork the king off a defensive square and collect the target.
notes.plans: Ng5+, then win e6.

notes.explains: Black's king walks into the pin, and the clinical punish is the rook takes e6 with check — but the check is just a bonus. The real point is that next comes the pawn to d5, winning the knight on c6 because its defender is pinned, and the whole queenside can stay home.
notes.teaches: Sacrifice to set up the follow-up: Rxe6+ then d5 wins the pinned knight.
notes.plans: Rxe6+, then d5.

notes.explains: The pawn to d5 is the game-winner — it wins the pinned knight, and once that minor piece falls the king is hunted down. White won't even need most of the queenside pieces; the already-active ones are that powerful.
notes.teaches: Cash the pin: winning the key defender collapses the whole position.
notes.plans: d5, win the knight, mate the king.

notes.explains: The finish is straightforward attacking chess: after the capture on c6 with check the knight defends the rook — that detail matters — and the king is dragged to c7. The bishop to f4 checks, and after the block the queen takes on d6 with checkmate.
notes.teaches: Bring even the sleeping pieces into a forced mating net once the king is stripped bare.
notes.plans: dxc6+, Bf4+, Qxd6 mate.

notes.explains: d4 opens the position to exploit the pin on the c6-knight — the Ruy's point against Steinitz's ...d6, prying the center while Black's king is still in it.
notes.teaches: Open the center to cash in a pin you've already established.

notes.explains: White voluntarily trades on c6 — surprising, since the pin was the pride of the position — but it softens the e5-pawn and clears the way to press the center.
notes.teaches: Surrender the bishop pair when the resulting pressure on the center outweighs the pin.

notes.explains: Nc3 completes development and adds a second guard to the center, building pressure before Black can fully coordinate against the tension.
notes.teaches: Finish developing with tempo, reinforcing your central squares.

notes.explains: Rather than a passive Exchange, Black strikes with e5 — accepting an isolated d-pawn in return for free, active piece play and the initiative. This is the fighting choice, not the quiet main line.
notes.teaches: You can answer the drawish Exchange with an e5 break, taking on an isolated pawn for activity.
notes.plans: Open the centre, activate the pieces, win the bishop pair.

notes.explains: After the trades the knight lands on e5, a fine central post, and Black is poised to win the bishop pair — the concrete pay-off for accepting the isolated pawn.
notes.teaches: An isolated queen's pawn buys active pieces and often the two bishops; that activity is the compensation.

notes.explains: The knight takes on d3 with check, handing Black the bishop pair — the long-term trump that justifies the isolated d-pawn.
notes.teaches: Trade a knight for the bishop holding the position together to bank the bishop pair.

notes.explains: The knight leaps into e4, striking the bishop on g5 and grabbing the center instead of meekly defending. This is the point against the Trompowsky — challenge the bishop at once.
notes.teaches: Meet an early bishop pin by counterattacking the pinning piece, not by passively unpinning.

notes.explains: Black answers in the centre with the pawn to e6, steering the game into a French — the solid, conceptual structure where the d5-pawn is backed by e6 and the fight is about the light squares.
notes.teaches: e6 turns a queen's-pawn move order into a French: the pawn on d5 gets a permanent defender.
notes.plans: Play on the light squares behind the d5/e6 chain.

notes.explains: And here is the small but significant slip: the knight to d7. It looks natural, but it stands directly in front of the queen and cuts off her defence of the d5-pawn down the file. That single detail hands White a clean pawn.
notes.teaches: A developing move that blocks your own piece's defence of a key pawn is a real error, not a nuance.
notes.plans: Punish by opening the centre while the pawn is undefended.

notes.explains: White cracks it open with the pawn takes on d5. The recapture is forced, and every route leads back to a d5-pawn that the knight on d7 has left to fend for itself.
notes.teaches: Open the position exactly where the opponent's coordination has broken down.
notes.plans: Trade on d5 and collect the loose pawn.

notes.explains: The knight simply takes on d5, winning the pawn. The queen on d8 would love to be guarding it, but her own knight on d7 is in the way — the flaw made concrete.
notes.teaches: When a defender is blocked, the target isn't defended — count the real guards, not the nominal ones.
notes.plans: Bank the pawn, then develop calmly.

notes.explains: Already a pawn up, there is no reason to reinvent the wheel — the knight takes on f6 and simplifies. Trading pieces while ahead in material sharpens the advantage rather than dulling it.
notes.teaches: When you're up material, trade pieces; the extra pawn matters more with fewer men on the board.
notes.plans: Simplify, finish development, convert.

notes.explains: The bishop belongs on d3, not b5. The pin on b5 looks tempting, but Black just plays the pawn to c6 and shrugs it off with a healthy central move. Pins are powerful and also the most over-rated idea in chess — this one costs a tempo for nothing.
notes.teaches: Don't over-value a pin the opponent can dissolve with a useful move; place the bishop where it stays active.
notes.plans: Aim the bishop at h7 and build toward the battery.

notes.explains: Castling first, keeping things circumspect — no wayward check on e8, king tucked away, and the c1-bishop left alone for now, since it already does plenty guarding the dark squares from home.
notes.teaches: Get the king safe before committing pieces; a piece that already covers key squares needn't move.
notes.plans: King safety first, then the attacking plan.

notes.explains: The pawn to c3 launches the standard plan: it props up the d4-pawn and clears the way for bishop-to-c2 and then queen-to-d3 — the queen in front of the bishop, because that way she leads the battery and carries the mate threat toward h7.
notes.teaches: Build the bishop-and-queen battery with the queen in front, so the queen delivers the threat and the bishop supports.
notes.plans: c3, Bc2, Qd3 aiming at h7.

notes.explains: Black's pawn has poked out to c4, sticking out like a sore thumb, and the textbook cure is to undermine it at the base with the pawn to b3. If it captures, the a-file opens and the intruder is gone.
notes.teaches: Undermine an over-extended pawn at its base rather than attacking the head of it.
notes.plans: b3 to dissolve or fix the c4-pawn.

notes.explains: First soften it with the capture on c4, so the pawn is no longer protected, and the knight can reroute back through d2 to pile up on the weakness. Keep the bishop right where it is on c2 — a4 would only distract it.
notes.teaches: Remove a weak pawn's protection first, then bring a rerouted piece to attack it.
notes.plans: Reroute the knight via d2 onto c4.

notes.explains: Here is the sting. The bishop on e4 and Black's rook on a8 sit on the same diagonal, screened only by the queen on g6 — an x-ray. Move the queen with a capture and the bishop's line springs open: the queen crashes into a8, taking the rook. Boom goes the dynamite.
notes.teaches: Behind a piece on an x-ray, remove the screen with tempo and the rear piece's power is unleashed.
notes.plans: Desperado the queen into a8, cashing the x-ray.

notes.explains: Loose pieces drop off — the rule that decides so many positions. With Black's pieces hanging, White is up a full rook. From here, converting means trades, not heroics: a pawn is worth giving to swap the last minor pieces, but avoid the unnecessary simplification that only helps the defender.
notes.teaches: When winning, trade toward a clear technical position and don't cling to every pawn; loose pieces drop off.
notes.plans: Trade pieces, keep the extra rook, convert.

notes.explains: The King's Gambit — f4 offers a pawn to blast open the f-file and seize the center, the oldest romantic attacking try in chess.
notes.teaches: Gambit a wing pawn to open lines and build a big center for a direct attack.

notes.explains: In the classical King's Gambit Black clings to the extra pawn with g5, propping up a pawn chain — but that chain is loose, and White strikes it with h4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent over-defends a gambit pawn on the wing, undermine the chain that supports it.

notes.explains: h4 hits the g5-pawn at once, prying open the h-file and refusing to let Black consolidate the extra pawn — the sharp, sacrificial soul of the opening.
notes.teaches: In sharp gambits, keep hitting the opponent's defensive pawns before they finish developing.

notes.explains: Recapturing with the d-pawn defines the Stafford — Black accepts doubled c-pawns in return for open lines, rapid development, and dangerous piece play against f2.
notes.teaches: Trade structural soundness for open lines and initiative in a gambit.

notes.explains: Bishop to c5 is the Stafford's fang — it rakes the a7-g1 diagonal straight at f2, the softest square in White's camp, setting up a swarm of tactics.
notes.teaches: Point your pieces at f2, the weakest square near the enemy king, to manufacture threats.

notes.explains: The knight jumps to g4, hitting h2 and swarming the weak squares around White's king that the early trades left tender — the initiative is in full flow.
notes.teaches: Pile jumping pieces onto the weakened squares near the king to keep the attack going.

notes.explains: The bishop to g5 is the Averbakh's sting. It means Black's natural e5 break now costs a pawn, because after the centre trades the pin on the knight on f6 tells — so Black is nudged into the slightly awkward h6.
notes.teaches: The Averbakh's bishop on g5 pre-empts Black's freeing e5 break by pinning the f6-knight.
notes.plans: Provoke h6, retreat the bishop to e3, then storm with g4 and h4.

notes.explains: When Black does play e5, White closes with d5 and the plan crystallizes: a kingside pawn storm, since the locked centre means White can hurl the g- and h-pawns forward without fear of a counterblow.
notes.teaches: With the centre locked, storm the wing where you hold the space.

notes.explains: Black's early e5 lets White trade queens into a pleasant endgame, a version of the Exchange King's Indian. White's edge is small but riskless: more space and the more comfortable pieces to nurse.
notes.teaches: An early queen trade can hand you a small, safe endgame pull to grind.

notes.explains: The knight to d5 is the star — a dominant central outpost Black cannot easily challenge, controlling key squares and cramping the whole black position.
notes.teaches: Plant a knight on d5, the outpost that defines White's edge in these structures.

notes.explains: White expands with g4, grabbing space and tightening the bind. In a better endgame you improve slowly, squeezing the opponent before you ever break.
notes.teaches: With a small edge, gain space and improve every piece before forcing matters.

notes.explains: Against the French the choice is the pawn to e5 with the knight to f3 — the Steinitz treatment of the Advance. No c3 to prop up d4; the whole system will revolve around the e5-pawn instead.
notes.teaches: Steinitz Advance: commit to e5 and Nf3, and plan to live without c3.
notes.plans: e5, Nf3, build around the clamp.

notes.explains: Black plays the bishop to d7 expecting c3 — but that move never comes. The point of the Steinitz is to leave the pawn on d4 to be taken, make every other normal French move, and simply save the tempo c3 would have cost.
notes.teaches: Conserve the c3 tempo — let d4 go and spend the time on development.
notes.plans: Bd3, castle, let d4 fall.

notes.explains: Before the knight comes to d2, the bishop drops to f4 to over-protect e5 — pile defenders on the clamp so it never becomes a worry. Everything in this system is in the service of that one pawn.
notes.teaches: Over-protect the key pawn first; a heavily-guarded clamp frees your other pieces.
notes.plans: Bf4, then Nbd2 without fear for e5.

notes.explains: The knight to d2, and the b2-pawn is simply left hanging. If Black grabs it, the rook to b1 rips open the b-file, and against a king this underdeveloped the file alone is a disaster — no calculation required.
notes.teaches: Offer a wing pawn when the recapture opens a file straight at an undeveloped opponent.
notes.plans: Nbd2; welcome ...Qxb2 Rb1.

notes.explains: Recapture on d3 with the pawn — taking with the queen would run into the bishop to b5, winning her. And the pawn recapture is what you'd want anyway: it opens the c-file for a rook.
notes.teaches: Choose the recapture that both avoids a pin and opens a file for your rooks.
notes.plans: cxd3, seize the c-file.

notes.explains: No rush to snatch d4. Contest the c-file first with the rook to c1 — the pawn isn't going anywhere, and grabbing it a move later loses nothing while the file is worth more now.
notes.teaches: Take the open file before collecting a pawn that can't run away.
notes.plans: Rc1, then win d4 at leisure.

notes.explains: Dropping the bishop back to e3 keeps the queenside pressure and, more importantly, sets up the real plan: the f-pawn marching f4 and f5 to blast open Black's kingside while his bishop still sleeps at home.
notes.teaches: Regroup with a purpose — Be3 clears the way for the f4-f5 pawn storm.
notes.plans: Be3, then f4-f5.

notes.explains: Simplest is to take on c6 — it deals with the ...Nxe5 idea, trades into a clean structure, and gains a tempo. In a rich position with many roughly equal options, the simple move is the strong one.
notes.teaches: Amid many equal choices, pick the one that neutralises the threat and simplifies.
notes.plans: Trade on c6, keep it clean.

notes.explains: White sidesteps with the knight to c3 rather than the main advance. The genuine Alekhine reply is the pawn to d5: pushing on into a Vienna is playable, but d5 steers into a favourable Scandinavian instead.
notes.teaches: When White declines the main line with Nc3, strike with d5 for a good Scandinavian structure.
notes.plans: Trade in the centre and reach a comfortable Scandi.

notes.explains: After the exchanges it is a Scandinavian with a key difference: White's knight is already gone from c3, so it can never harass the queen with tempo. The queen sits comfortably in the centre.
notes.teaches: A Scandinavian where White's knight has left c3 is ideal — the exposed queen is never chased.
notes.plans: Develop actively behind the safe central queen.

notes.explains: Develop with the bishop to g4 and the knight to c6, then castle queenside — a harmonious, aggressive setup with the pieces pointing at White's position.
notes.teaches: Rapid development plus opposite-wing castling turns a solid structure into an attacking one.
notes.plans: Castle long and open lines toward White's king.

notes.explains: Because White has set up passively with the pawn on d3, the thrust e5 makes good sense — grab as much central space as possible while White is cramped.
notes.teaches: Against a passive setup, expand in the centre and take the space on offer.
notes.plans: Build the centre, then storm the kingside.

notes.explains: Nxe5 launches the center fork trick — White briefly sacrifices the knight, knowing that after the recapture, d4 forks the bishop and knight to win the piece straight back.
notes.teaches: The center fork trick sacs a knight to regain it with a pawn fork and a superior center.

notes.explains: White plays the Averbakh with the bishop on g5 and immediately lunges h4. The intent is a raw kingside pawn storm: Black's king is his only home, and the h-file will be the highway to it.
notes.teaches: The Averbakh can be a direct attacking weapon — h4 first, questions later.
notes.plans: Push g4, g5 and h5 to prise open the h-file.

notes.explains: Black strikes with e5 and White closes with d5. The centre locked and Black's king committed, White is free to hurl everything at the kingside — the classic closed-centre attack.
notes.teaches: Lock the centre, then storm the wing where the enemy king sits.

notes.explains: The pawn reaches h5, cracking open the h-file straight at Black's king — the whole reason for committing the h-pawn so early.
notes.teaches: A wing pawn storm's goal is to lever open a file against the castled king.

notes.explains: After Black's c6 and d5, White braces e4 with f3 and keeps the big pawn chain — the standard clamp against the Gurgenidze, holding a broad centre.
notes.teaches: Meet the c6-and-d5 Gurgenidze by shoring up e4 with f3 and keeping the full centre.
notes.plans: Hold the centre, develop, and castle long.

notes.explains: Black's e5 break comes too early. After White captures, Black is simply worse — the centre opens in White's favour with far better development.
notes.teaches: Don't strike in the centre before you're developed; a premature break just hands the opponent a lead.

notes.explains: Trading queens looks like it should ease Black's game, but it does the opposite: the king is dragged to d8, loses the right to castle, and stays stuck in the centre while White pours out pieces.
notes.teaches: A queen trade favours the side whose king it does not strand — here Black loses castling and stays exposed.

notes.explains: The bishop to c4 and long castling complete a crushing setup: every white piece is out and aimed at the stranded black king, while Black can barely untangle.
notes.teaches: Convert a development lead by finishing development and castling before the opponent can catch up.

notes.explains: Here is the surprise: the fianchetto with the pawn to g3. It looks modest, but it is an easy, low-theory system against the Qa5 Scandinavian that catches many players off guard.
notes.teaches: A quiet fianchetto setup can be a practical weapon precisely because opponents don't prepare for it.
notes.plans: Fianchetto, develop, and target the c6-pawn.

notes.explains: The knight develops to e2, not f3 — deliberately, so it does not block the g2-bishop. White's whole plan is to break down Black's c6-pawn and open the long diagonal for that bishop.
notes.teaches: Develop the knight to e2 to keep the fianchettoed bishop's diagonal clear.
notes.plans: Prepare the b-pawn advance to hit c6.

notes.explains: Meet the bishop pin on b4 with the simple pawn to a3. It is a natural response, and it fits the plan — the b-pawn is on its way to b4 and b5, a minority attack against c6.
notes.teaches: a3 both questions the pinning bishop and clears the path for the b-pawn's advance.
notes.plans: Push b4-b5 to undermine c6.

notes.explains: Against the bishop coming to g4, do NOT weaken with f3 — instead the queen steps to e1, unpinning quietly and keeping the queenside plan rolling.
notes.teaches: Answer a pin with a repositioning move, not a weakening pawn push.
notes.plans: Continue the b-pawn minority attack.

notes.explains: White's h4 signals a kingside pawn storm, and Black stops it cold with h5, freezing the h-pawn before it can lever the h-file open. With the attack out of fuel, Black turns to his own play.
notes.teaches: Meet a wing pawn storm by blocking it — a frozen h-pawn cannot open the file.
notes.plans: Trade off White's active pieces, then expand with b5.

notes.explains: The knight on e5 is White's most active piece and the seed of the kingside attack, so Black hurries to trade it off with the knight to d7 — remove the attacker and the initiative fizzles.
notes.teaches: Neutralize an attack by trading off its key piece.

notes.explains: With the kingside shut, Black rolls the queenside pawns — b5 and then b4 — opening lines against White's king, which is still stuck in the centre. The Barry's slow setup gives Black exactly that time.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king is uncastled, pry open lines against it with a pawn advance.

notes.explains: g3 sets up the Glek — the bishop heads to g2 to bear down the long diagonal, a flexible fianchetto system that steers the open games into fresh, less-charted waters.
notes.teaches: Choose a fianchetto system to sidestep mainstream theory and press the long diagonal.

notes.explains: King to h2 is prophylactic — it tucks the king away and, crucially, defends the h3-pawn so the knight can reroute to d2 and the f-pawn can advance with no loose ends.
notes.teaches: A quiet king move can shore up a pawn and free your pieces for the coming plan.

notes.explains: Against the McDonnell's early f4, Black hits back with d5 at once — the standard antidote. Strike the centre before White completes the setup, and refuse to let the flank push dictate the game.
notes.teaches: Meet an early f4 flank push with a central d5 counter-strike.

notes.explains: The knight rounds up the last pawn and Black emerges from the opening comfortably: the McDonnell's aggression has fizzled, and Black is at least equal.
notes.teaches: Neutralize a gambit-style attack by returning its aggression and regaining the pawn cleanly.

notes.explains: The pieces swarm White's overstretched position, and the knight to g4 forks the rook on f2 and the queen on e3 — the small opening edge has grown into a winning material advantage.
notes.teaches: Sustained pressure eventually springs a fork that converts the initiative into material.

notes.explains: This is the Grünfeld — d5 meets the center head-on, striking c4 and daring White to build a broad pawn center that Black will then chip away at from the wings.
notes.teaches: The hypermodern idea: let White occupy the center, then dismantle it with pieces and timely pawn breaks.

notes.explains: The thematic c5 strikes at White's d4-pawn, prying at the center before it can settle. A knight to c6 would let White reinforce with e3 — the pawn break is far sharper.
notes.teaches: Undermine the base of the opponent's center with a pawn break rather than a slow piece hit.

notes.explains: Knight takes c3 and the game is essentially decided. White muddled two different setups, and now the knight forks the queen on d1; once the queens come off, the bishop crashes in with check.
notes.teaches: Punish a mixed-up move order with the concrete tactic it allows — here a knight fork through the center.

notes.explains: The knight jumps into d4, offering to trade White's defender on f3 and turning the whole army toward the king. Forget regaining pawns — this is a mating attack.
notes.teaches: When far ahead in development, ignore material and pile pieces onto the exposed king.

notes.explains: Rook takes c5 with check, tearing the c-file wide open at the king on c1. The bishop on d4 joins the rook and White's king has nowhere left to run.
notes.teaches: Give up pawns without a thought to keep lines crashing open against a stranded king.

notes.explains: d4 strikes the center at once — against Black's passive ...d6 Berlin, opening lines exploits the lag rather than allowing a slow, solid setup.
notes.teaches: Open the center against a passive defense to make your development lead count.

notes.explains: Capturing on c6 keeps the knight proudly centralized on d4 while saddling Black with doubled, damaged queenside pawns — a lasting structural plus.
notes.teaches: Trade bishop for knight to inflict permanent pawn weaknesses while keeping your best piece.

notes.explains: d4 is the heart of the Four Knights Scotch — with every piece developing naturally, White opens the center on sound principles, no gimmicks.
notes.teaches: The Scotch Four Knights fights for the center by principle, not by trick.

notes.explains: Recapturing on d4 with the bishop leaves White the two bishops and a firm grip on the center — Black's early trade only handed over those long-term assets.
notes.teaches: An opponent's premature trade can gift you the bishop pair and central control.

notes.explains: f3 reinforces the e4-pawn and readies a kingside storm with g4 and h4 — with kings on opposite wings, White races to prise open Black's king.
notes.teaches: Bolster your center with f3, then storm the wing where the enemy king has castled.

notes.explains: Bishop to g4 pins the knight on f3 and lays a trap — after h3 the bishop simply stays, provoking the weakening g4 and handing Black targets around White's king.
notes.teaches: Pin an enemy knight to bait a loosening pawn advance in front of the king.

notes.explains: Retreating to b6 keeps the bishop and sidesteps a trade on c5 that would have handed White the two bishops — Black holds onto both bishops and the tension.
notes.teaches: Retreat a bishop to dodge a trade that would concede the bishop pair.

notes.explains: The bishop slides to h5, keeping the pin alive after h3 and daring White to play g4 — every provoked pawn move opens another seam near the white king.
notes.teaches: Maintain a pin along the diagonal to keep provoking committal pawn moves.

notes.explains: The modest d3 sidesteps the sharp Ng5 tricks and steers into a quiet Italian-style setup — no theory to memorize, just sound development and a pleasant position.
notes.teaches: Choose a calm pawn-and-piece setup to reach a comfortable middlegame without forcing lines.

notes.explains: h3 pre-empts a bishop coming to g4 — a key prophylactic move before castling, since once the king is on g1 that pin becomes far more dangerous.
notes.teaches: Play h3 before short castling to deny the enemy bishop the g4 pin.

notes.explains: With Black tangled up preparing ...f5, d4 strikes to open the center — the textbook answer to a wing plan is a blow in the middle.
notes.teaches: Meet a slow flank plan by opening the center where you're better developed.

notes.explains: d4 hits e5 at once — the Center Game and Danish family, offering to open the position fast and drag Black into a fight before development is complete.
notes.teaches: Challenge e5 with d4 to open the center immediately.

notes.explains: The queen boldly takes d4, centralizing and eyeing the knight on e5 and the bishop on b4 together — aggressive and committal, bending opening rules for concrete pressure.
notes.teaches: A centralized queen can be strong early if it makes real threats faster than it can be harassed.

notes.explains: White's move order is slightly odd, but the recipe is simple: play whatever Sicilian you normally play. The knight to c6 keeps every standard setup available.
notes.teaches: Against an offbeat move order, transpose into your familiar main lines — don't be thrown.
notes.plans: Develop naturally toward your usual structure.

notes.explains: Develop the knight to f6, adding a piece and pressing on the e4-pawn. With the pieces coming out actively, Black is comfortable against the passive bishop setup.
notes.teaches: Develop with pressure on the centre — the knight on f6 hits e4 and readies the freeing break.
notes.plans: Prepare a central break and equalise.

notes.explains: The French, and against it the pawn to e5 — the Advance. The clamp goes up and Black must find counterplay against it.
notes.teaches: e5 is the thematic Advance clamp against the French.
notes.plans: e5, then support the chain.

notes.explains: Instead of the main move c5, Black tries the pawn to b6 — an old sideline. The whole idea is the bishop to a6, to swap off the light-squared bishop that the French normally leaves boxed in behind e6.
notes.teaches: Against the Advance, ...b6 aims to trade Black's bad light-squared bishop via ...Ba6.
notes.plans: Prevent or punish the bishop trade.

notes.explains: The pawn to c3 quietly does two jobs. It props up d4 — and it clears the d1-a4 diagonal, so that if the bishop comes to a6, White captures and then the queen to a4 checks the king while forking the knight on a6.
notes.teaches: c3 opens the d1-a4 diagonal: ...Ba6 Bxa6 Nxa6 Qa4+ forks king and knight.
notes.plans: c3, then meet ...Ba6 with the Qa4+ fork.

notes.explains: With the bishop trade defused, just develop nicely — the bishop to d3, taking a good diagonal and preparing to castle.
notes.teaches: Once the opponent's key idea is stopped, develop by principle.
notes.plans: Bd3, castle, then attack.

notes.explains: The knight goes to e2, not f3 — deliberately. Keeping the f-pawn free lets it charge f4 and f5 later, and that pawn on e6 is exactly the target the storm will crash into.
notes.teaches: Develop the knight to e2 to keep the f-pawn free for the f4-f5 break against e6.
notes.plans: Ne2, later f4-f5.

notes.explains: Don't rush the f-pawn — castle and complete the setup first. Black is grabbing queenside space instead of developing, which is the signal to finish preparing and then hit the gas with f4.
notes.teaches: Complete development before launching the pawn storm; punish an undeveloping opponent by speeding up.
notes.plans: O-O, then f4 toward f5.

notes.explains: c3 is the quiet linchpin of the Ruy — it prepares the central advance d4 and hands the b3-bishop a retreat on c2, unhurried and deeply positional.
notes.teaches: Prepare your central break with a modest pawn move that also frees a retreat for your key bishop.

notes.explains: Finally d4 breaks in the center — the whole point of the slow c3 build-up, challenging e5 and opening lines for the bishops.
notes.teaches: After the preparatory moves, strike with the central break you've been readying.

notes.explains: The knights come out to f6 and f3 — the deeply-studied main line. Everything so far is theory, and Black stands at a major crossroads with several sound tries.
notes.teaches: The Qxd5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 tabiya is heavily analysed — know the branches, don't improvise.
notes.plans: Complete development and keep the small pull.

notes.explains: Capturing on c5 is double-edged: it allows Black to trade queens and drag White's king into the centre. Many players avoid it for that reason, but the resulting queenless middlegame is fully playable.
notes.teaches: A capture that trades queens and exposes your king isn't bad — just know the endgame is the real battle.
notes.plans: Accept the king walk; the extra structure compensates.

notes.explains: After the queens come off and the king recaptures on d1, the position turns sharp and technical — a queenless middlegame where accurate play, not memorised theory, decides.
notes.teaches: A king in the centre is fine with queens off — activity and accuracy matter more than castling.
notes.plans: Activate the pieces and hold the extra pawn.

notes.explains: The knight heads to a3 and onward to b5 — from there it eyes the c7-square and cramps Black's queenside, turning the sharp position into a lasting squeeze.
notes.teaches: Reroute the knight via a3-b5 to hit c7 and pressure the queenside.
notes.plans: Land the knight on b5 and press c7.

notes.explains: White has deliberately given up the bishop on a6 — a huge handicap taken on purpose. The whole game is a lesson in generating attacking chances from a lost position: develop fast and create complications.
notes.teaches: When down material by design, seek activity and complications rather than passive defense.

notes.explains: d4 stakes a claim in the center — down a piece, White must fight for space and open lines, and Black's passive ...d6 with the offside knight on a6 offers real practical chances.
notes.teaches: Build a strong center to turn a material deficit into attacking initiative.

notes.explains: Bishop to e3 shores up a solid pawn-and-piece center and prepares to castle long — the plan is to castle opposite Black and race a pawn storm at his king.
notes.teaches: Castle on the opposite wing from your opponent to launch a mutual pawn-storm race.

notes.explains: Occupy the centre with d4 and develop with the knight to f3 — a maximally flexible move. This knight never needs the passive e2-square, so f3 keeps every option open.
notes.teaches: Develop where the piece is both active and flexible — Nf3, not the passive Ne2.
notes.plans: Complete development and support the big centre.

notes.explains: This is a good moment to release the central tension by capturing on d4. Left alone, the advancing pawn mass could push the knights around, so White clarifies the centre on his own terms.
notes.teaches: Resolve central tension when leaving it lets the opponent's pawns gain space with tempo.
notes.plans: Fix the centre, then develop toward the kingside.

notes.explains: Bishop to c5 is the practical choice against the Scotch — it hits the knight on d4 and develops actively, dodging the heavy theory of ...Nf6.
notes.teaches: Pick an active, less-theoretical developing move to sidestep the opponent's preparation.

notes.explains: Queen to f6 doubles the pressure on d4 and quietly parries the Nxc6-then-Bxc5 fork — active without exposing itself.
notes.teaches: Add a second attacker to a target while defusing the opponent's tactical trick.

notes.explains: Taking on e3 first is the key in-between move — it wrecks White's structure and, after fxe3, uncorks a Qh4+ fork, so Black wins back the knight with a superior position.
notes.teaches: Insert an in-between capture that damages structure before you recapture.

notes.explains: The pawn to c3 prepared this: the pawn to d4, building the classical centre. And in these lines the knight already on c6 is often misplaced, because White will recapture on d4 with a pawn and get a mobile centre the knight can't easily blockade.
notes.teaches: c3 exists to support d4 — and an early Nc6 can misplace itself against the resulting pawn centre.
notes.plans: Take the centre and use its mobility.

notes.explains: When Black strikes with d5, take it with the pawn — do NOT push e5. Locking the centre with e5 would concede an inferior French where Black's light-squared bishop has already escaped outside the chain.
notes.teaches: Capture on d5 rather than closing with e5 — a French where the bad bishop is already free is a poor version.
notes.plans: Open the centre and play against the isolani.

notes.explains: After the queen recaptures on d5, the position is the standard Alapin tabiya — reached here by the Nc6 move order, but the same familiar isolated-pawn battleground.
notes.teaches: Recognise the transposition into the main isolated-pawn structure regardless of move order.
notes.plans: Blockade d5, trade pieces, target the isolani.

notes.explains: Against the Trompowsky's bishop on g5, Black hits back with the knight to e4, attacking the bishop at once and refusing to let White dictate. It is the most testing reply.
notes.teaches: Meet the Trompowsky's g5-bishop by jumping the knight to e4 to harass it immediately.

notes.explains: Black opens the centre: after the c5 break and recapture, the bishop lands actively on c5, and Black is already better developed than White's passive knights on d2 and e2.
notes.teaches: Open the centre when you are better developed and the opponent has spent time on the flank.

notes.explains: The pressure tells: with the dark-squared bishop traded off, the queen rakes the long diagonal and snatches b2. Black is up material with the initiative, and the Trompowsky is thoroughly refuted here.
notes.teaches: A queen on the long diagonal against a loose b2 is a standing invitation to grab material.

notes.explains: Drop the bishop back to e2 — the familiar idea, keeping Black's blocking bishop stuck awkwardly on d7 instead of trading it off.
notes.teaches: Preserve the opponent's bad bishop by declining the exchange.
notes.plans: Recover the pawn and take the centre.

notes.explains: The pawn to e6, trying to win back the d5-pawn, is the trap — it simply drops a pawn. Because the bishop already sits clumsily on d7, the recapture doesn't work cleanly.
notes.teaches: A recapture that relies on a badly-placed piece can just hang the pawn — check the tactics first.
notes.plans: Take on e6 and stay a pawn up.

notes.explains: A pawn to the good with no compensation for Black, and now the centre goes to d4. Simple, solid, and clearly better — the whole point of the b5-check paid off.
notes.teaches: Once ahead in material, occupy the centre and develop soundly.
notes.plans: Finish development and convert.

notes.explains: The pawn on c4 hands the knight a potential outpost on d4 — but there is no rush to sit on it. The knight comes to c6 first; the d4-hole is a long-term weakness that will tell only once everything is developed.
notes.teaches: A hole is a permanent asset — occupy it when the rest of your pieces are ready, not on move one.
notes.plans: Develop first; the d4 outpost keeps.

notes.explains: The fianchetto goes in. It concedes one thing — White can answer with the pawn to d4 and steer into a standard Maróczy Bind — but in return the g7-bishop gets a magnificent long diagonal.
notes.teaches: Every setup has a trade-off; here g6 allows a transposition but earns the Dragon's best piece.
notes.plans: Fianchetto and fight for the dark squares.

notes.explains: With the bishop on g7 Black is already comfortably better: the dark squares in the centre are dominated, and White's light-squared bishop is stuck behind its own c4-, d3- and e4-pawns — a big pawn, not a piece.
notes.teaches: A bishop hemmed in by its own fixed pawns is dead weight; play against it.
notes.plans: Trade the good pieces, leave White the bad bishop.

notes.explains: The pawn to d6 improves the position and, more to the point, prepares to trade off the f3-knight with the bishop to g4 — the knight is White's main guard of the d4 square. The g8-knight can wait.
notes.teaches: Target the piece defending your key square; here the f3-knight guards d4.
notes.plans: Play Bg4 to remove the d4 defender.

notes.explains: The bishop steps to g4, clamping down on d4 by threatening to trade the very piece that controls it. This is classic positional chess — remove the defender of the square you want.
notes.teaches: To win a square, trade off its defender.
notes.plans: Exchange on f3, then dominate d4.

notes.explains: Eliminate the knight while the chance is there. Trading the light-squared bishops is only fine for Black, but removing White's f3-knight — the guard of d4 — is the real prize, so take it now before it can slip away.
notes.teaches: Prefer the trade that removes the opponent's most useful piece, even at the cost of your own good one.
notes.plans: Own d4 uncontested.

notes.explains: The Botvinnik setup: fianchetto plus the pawn to e6, carving out e7 as the developing square for the g8-knight. The pawns stand like teeth, gripping the central light squares White can never occupy.
notes.teaches: The Botvinnik pawn structure (pawns on e6/d6/c5 with a fianchetto) clamps the central light squares.
notes.plans: Route the knight via e7 and keep the clamp.

notes.explains: No need to rush the pawn to d5 with nothing developed yet — the simplest is to get the knight to f3. Once the pieces are out, the central breaks d5 and e5 become real; premature, they're just concrete for its own sake.
notes.teaches: Finish development before committing to a concrete central break.
notes.plans: Develop first, break in the centre later.

notes.explains: Black's pawn to d6 is another passive, unforcing choice. Play it as primitively as possible — the knight to c3, keeping it in the spirit of e4. The pawn to c4 would be reasonable, but that's really a queen's-pawn way of playing.
notes.teaches: In an e4 opening, natural piece development beats grabbing extra space with c4.
notes.plans: Nc3, Bd3, castle, then strike.

notes.explains: The bishop to d3 is the square I want: it reinforces the e4-pawn and, once Black castles, prepares the pawn to e5 with the bishop staring at h7. The queen later joins on e4 — bishop and queen aimed at h7 is a real mate threat. Note the point: even when the h-pawn moves, the square it left behind stays weak.
notes.teaches: A moved pawn can fix nothing — the square it vacated may be the lasting weakness.
notes.plans: Bd3 then Qe4, battery on the b1-h7 diagonal.

notes.explains: Castle and keep making the most standard moves — the knight jump to b4 isn't even a threat, since the bishop just steps back and a3 shoos it away. Black's pawn to b6 ignores the kingside, and that's what invites punishment: to punish slow development you open the centre, because open files are direct pathways to the king and to loose pieces.
notes.teaches: Punishing slow development means opening the centre — files are highways to the king and to loose pieces.
notes.plans: Castle, then break to open lines.

notes.explains: This is the dynamite: the pawn to d5. The d6- and e6-pawns are hooks, and advancing onto them forces the centre open. Two moves do the job, but only this one opens the file I actually want — the e-file, the direct path to Black's king.
notes.teaches: Advance onto the opponent's pawn hooks to force the file you want open — here, the e-file.
notes.plans: d5 to rip open the e-file.

notes.explains: Recapturing on d5 completes the operation — the e-file is open straight at Black's uncastled king, and this is exactly why castling early mattered: the rook is already home to use the file the moment it opens.
notes.teaches: Castle early so your rook is ready to seize the file the instant the centre opens.
notes.plans: Use the open e-file against the stuck king.

notes.explains: Now the objective crystallises: keep Black's king in the centre. It's hard to shoot a moving target — if the king reaches the kingside the attack restarts from zero. The rook to e1 pins the bishop the moment it appears, chaining the king to its defence.
notes.teaches: Against a stuck king, prevent castling and pin its would-be defenders to keep it exposed.
notes.plans: Re1, pile on the pin, keep the king central.

notes.explains: First the bishop checks from b5, sidestepping a trade headache — and this light-squared bishop is worth keeping, because Black's pawn to b6 punched holes all over the light squares that only this piece can occupy.
notes.teaches: Preserve the bishop that patrols the colour complex your opponent has weakened.
notes.plans: Keep the light bishop, target the light-square holes.

notes.explains: After the trade on d7 the queen recaptures, and here's the second flaw: the knight sitting on b4 is loose. The open e-file was never the whole story — a stranded minor piece plus an exposed king is the raw material for a fork.
notes.teaches: Scan for two weaknesses at once — an open line and a loose piece combine into a decisive tactic.
notes.plans: Kick the knight, then fork it with the king.

notes.explains: The pawn to a3 shoves the knight, and you want to do this regardless of the follow-up: a minor piece parked on your side of the board is a target for pawns. It has to trudge back to a6, and now it's really out of play.
notes.teaches: Push away an intruding minor piece with a pawn — offside knights are pawn-fodder.
notes.plans: a3 to sideline the knight onto a6.

notes.explains: There it is — the queen to e2 with check. Forget the e-file for a second: this checks the king and, on the same move, rakes the a6-knight down the diagonal. Loose pieces drop off — an exposed king plus an undefended piece is a ready-made fork, and White wins the knight and the game.
notes.teaches: Loose piece + open king = fork; one move that checks and attacks the stray piece wins it.
notes.plans: Qe2+, then capture the loose knight.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to d3, its most natural square, eyeing the kingside. Simple, principled development before the central tension arrives.
notes.teaches: Develop the bishop to its best diagonal before the middlegame breaks.
notes.plans: Bd3, then meet ...c5 with c3.

notes.explains: And here, unlike in the Nimzowitsch line, White does play the pawn to c3. Don't confuse this with the Advance proper — it's a common French structure, but the piece configurations are very different.
notes.teaches: In the Tarrasch, c3 supports d4; the resulting play differs from the Advance despite the pawn shape.
notes.plans: c3, hold the centre, develop.

notes.explains: Once more the pawn to f3, the Fantasy: keep the centre and play for space and a squeeze rather than a theoretical duel.
notes.teaches: f3 holds the centre and steers toward a positional space game.

notes.explains: Against the passive knight to d7, White pushes e5 and claims a broad space edge. The position takes on a French-Advance character, with the d4-e5 chain cramping Black.
notes.teaches: Meet a passive setup by grabbing space with e5 and playing a pawn-chain squeeze.
notes.plans: Buttress the chain with c3 and f4, then attack.

notes.explains: The pawn to f4 reinforces e5 and grabs maximum kingside space — the classic chain advance. It shuts in the c1-bishop for now, but the room to attack is worth it.
notes.teaches: Expand the pawn chain with f4 for space, accepting a temporarily passive bishop.

notes.explains: The pawn to c4 prepares to crack the centre open at the right moment. White has maxed out space and now wants to open lines where Black is still underdeveloped.
notes.teaches: Open the position only once your space and development lead is real.

notes.explains: The space edge cashes in: with Black's king stuck in the centre, the knight jumps to e5 with check and the hunt begins.
notes.teaches: A space advantage converts to a direct attack when the enemy king is stranded in the middle.

notes.explains: With the knight already on c6 and the pawn to d6, Black steers into an offbeat Nimzowitsch/Philidor-flavoured setup. White simply builds the centre with d4 and enjoys more space.
notes.teaches: Against the Nimzowitsch Defense, occupy the centre — the offbeat move order concedes space.
notes.plans: Build the big centre and develop.

notes.explains: Black's bishop to g4 pins the knight, but it is a fairly toothless try. Rather than tolerate it, the bishop to b5 sidesteps the whole idea and pins Black's own knight in return.
notes.teaches: Answer a weak pin by creating a stronger counter-pin rather than passively unpinning.
notes.plans: Increase the pressure on c6.

notes.explains: The capture on c6 damages Black's pawn structure — the doubled, weakened pawns become long-term targets while White keeps the freer position.
notes.teaches: Trade to inflict a structural weakness when you can pressure it afterward.
notes.plans: Play against the doubled pawns with the better development.

notes.explains: Nc3 is the Vienna Game — a flexible developing move that keeps the aggressive f4 gambit in reserve against Black's e5.
notes.teaches: The Vienna develops the queenside knight first, holding the f-pawn thrust back as a weapon.

notes.explains: f4 is the Vienna Gambit — striking at e5 even with the bishop on c5, offering a pawn to blast open the f-file and seize a big center.
notes.teaches: Gambit the f-pawn to open lines and grab the center for a kingside attack.

notes.explains: Nf3 develops with a crucial purpose — it snuffs out the annoying Qh4+ that would fork the king and the loose f-pawn, keeping the initiative in hand.
notes.teaches: Develop pieces to squares that shut down the opponent's checks and forks.

notes.explains: The pawn to e6 is the solid main line, reaching a famous, deeply-studied theoretical position — Black shores up d5 and prepares normal development.
notes.teaches: e6 is the reliable Alapin main line, a sound small-centre setup for Black.
notes.plans: Develop harmoniously; White will manoeuvre for the squeeze.

notes.explains: The knight route to a3 and then c4 is the heart of White's squeeze — heading for the b6- and d6-outposts and cramping Black's queenside. This is how you throttle the Sicilian slowly.
notes.teaches: The Na3-Nc4 manoeuvre targets b6/d6 — a positional clamp on Black's queenside.
notes.plans: Land the knight on c4 and press the weak dark squares.

notes.explains: Black defends the b6-square the right way — with the knight to d7, guarding while developing. Both jobs in one move.
notes.teaches: Meet a positional threat with a move that also develops, not a passive pawn move.
notes.plans: (For White:) restrict with a4 and keep squeezing.

notes.explains: The greedy capture on g2 is the trap: it runs straight into the bishop to f3, which traps the queen's escape and hands White a massive initiative and full compensation for the pawn.
notes.teaches: Grabbing g2 with the queen often loses to Bf3 skewering it against the rook — count before you grab.
notes.plans: (Black must instead break with e5.)

notes.explains: The pawn to c4 is the Panov Attack — rather than a quiet Exchange, White challenges d5 at once and steers into a sharp, tactical fight built around an isolated queen's pawn.
notes.teaches: The Panov turns the Exchange Caro into an aggressive IQP battle.
notes.plans: Pressure d5, accept an isolated d-pawn for space and active pieces.

notes.explains: Black releases the tension and White recaptures on c4, reaching the famous isolated queen's-pawn structure: the d4-pawn now stands alone, a long-term weakness but the source of open lines and piece activity.
notes.teaches: The IQP is a two-sided bargain — a weak pawn traded for space and active pieces.

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to f5 before a later e6 would shut it in. The middlegame theme is set: White leans on the d4-pawn's space while both sides fight over d5, the blockade square right in front of the isolated pawn.
notes.teaches: With an isolated queen's pawn, the square in front of it decides everything — control d5 and the pawn is a spearhead; blockade it and the pawn is a target.

notes.explains: White clamps with the pawn to c4, trying to hang on to the extra central pawn and cramp Black. It is an underrated try that needs a precise response.
notes.teaches: A c4 clamp holding an extra pawn must be met actively, not passively.
notes.plans: Strike back to unlock full compensation.

notes.explains: The key is the pawn to e6, undermining the d5-wedge to unlock the compensation. White has to take, and Black recaptures with the bishop, emerging with fast, active development for the pawn.
notes.teaches: Sacrifice a tempo/pawn with e6 to open lines and activate the pieces — development is the compensation.
notes.plans: Recapture with the bishop and develop with pressure.

notes.explains: With the knight to c6 Black grips the key central squares, making it genuinely hard for White to untangle and develop. The initiative, not the pawn count, defines the position.
notes.teaches: When down a pawn for activity, clamp the squares that keep the opponent tangled.
notes.plans: Keep the pieces active and the white king stuck in the centre.

notes.explains: Bishop to g4 pins the knight on f3 — with the e5-pawn firmly held, Black leans on the bishop pair to create pressure and tie White's pieces down.
notes.teaches: Use a bishop pin to restrain the opponent's knight and exploit the two bishops.

notes.explains: Bishop to d6 is the classic Exchange setup — it guards e5 and eyes the kingside, completing a harmonious, solid deployment for Black.
notes.teaches: Place the dark-squared bishop where it both defends the center and points at the enemy king.

notes.explains: Bishop takes on f6 shatters Black's kingside — even at the cost of the bishop pair, it strips the defender and cripples any pawn cover around the king.
notes.teaches: Trade a bishop to wreck the pawn shield in front of a king you mean to attack.

notes.explains: Knight to d5 leaps to the outpost with the black king and queen sitting on awkward, exposed squares — Black is in deep trouble.
notes.teaches: Occupy a central outpost with tempo when the enemy king and queen are poorly placed.

notes.explains: White's f4 sets up the Four Pawns Attack — the most space-grabbing anti-King's-Indian line, with pawns on c4, d4, e4 and f4. It is dangerous but overextended, and Black must strike at that wall before it rolls forward.
notes.teaches: Against the Four Pawns' huge centre, counter-strike quickly — an overextended centre is a target.
notes.plans: Hit the centre with e5 or c5.

notes.explains: Black strikes at once with e5, hitting the base of the pawn wall. It looks reckless into all that space, but it forces White to resolve the tension and pries the overextension open.
notes.teaches: Undermine a broad pawn centre by challenging it immediately, before it becomes a rolling force.

notes.explains: Knight to f6 is the sound reply — it counterattacks e4 at once, treating the Bishop's Opening just like a Vienna and refusing to be intimidated.
notes.teaches: Answer a slow bishop development by hitting the center with ...Nf6.

notes.explains: Bishop to e7 is the solid Hungarian setup — modest but rock-solid, leaving Black no weaknesses and a comfortable position to hold.
notes.teaches: Choose a compact, weakness-free deployment when you value solidity over activity.

notes.explains: Bishop to e6 offers to trade off White's active light bishop; if White takes, recapturing with the f-pawn hands Black the half-open f-file to attack down.
notes.teaches: Challenge the opponent's good bishop, and welcome a recapture that opens a file for your rooks.

notes.explains: The pawn to f4 — the Four Pawns Attack, objectively one of the very best tries against the Alekhine. If White knows the follow-up, White is simply better, and the pressure is immediate.
notes.teaches: The Four Pawns is the most testing anti-Alekhine — a genuine attempt at an opening advantage, not just a gambit.
notes.plans: Hold the giant centre and develop into the attack.

notes.explains: Recapture toward the centre with the f-pawn — NOT with the d-pawn, which would invite an unfavourable queen trade. The plus of the whole system is a monster centre; the minus is lagging development, so precision is required.
notes.teaches: Recapture toward the centre to keep the pawn mass and avoid a queen trade that relieves the defender.
notes.plans: Complete the centre, then catch up in development.

notes.explains: Restraint again: the knight to f3 would allow the bishop pin on g4 with heavy pressure on the centre, and the pawn to d5 would simply drop e5. The bishop to e3 is the sound way to defend the pawn.
notes.teaches: Defend the centre with a developing move that avoids the pin — the bishop to e3.
notes.plans: Develop the queen's knight, then the king's knight when safe.

notes.explains: Collect the loosened knight with the bishop on b6. The point of the earlier d5 is realised — a concrete gain, converting the central pressure into material.
notes.teaches: Follow a well-timed break to its concrete payoff — the win of the undersupported piece.
notes.plans: Consolidate the extra material and press the centre.
