notes.explains: After the f7 sacrifice, White's queen grabs the bishop on c5 with check — but the king is best on f8, tucked off the e-file where it's temporarily safe from the coming pressure.
notes.teaches: When your king is exposed, choose the square that shelters it from the most dangerous open lines.

notes.explains: With the king weak, Black's priority is rapid development — Nf6 hits e4 and brings a piece out toward the plan of castling by hand.
notes.teaches: When your king is caught in the center, develop with tempo and race to shelter it.

notes.explains: The king finally reaches g8 — Black has castled by hand, walking the king to safety one step at a time and weathering the storm from the sacrifice.
notes.teaches: Reroute an exposed king to a safe corner manually when normal castling is gone.

notes.explains: The pawn to c3 against the accelerated-dragon move order sets up the Alapin — but with Black's knight already on c6, the usual d5-break loses some of its point, and White gets to fight for a broad centre.
notes.teaches: Move order matters: with the knight already on c6, Black's d5 break is less effective.
notes.plans: Prepare d4 and claim the centre.

notes.explains: If Black answers with the pawn to e5, it creates a big hole on d5 — a lasting weakness. White strikes at the centre with d4 in Italian style, opening lines against the loosened position.
notes.teaches: A pawn to e5 that leaves a hole on d5 is a long-term concession — occupy the outpost.
notes.plans: Break with d4 and exploit the d5-hole.

notes.explains: d4 is the Scotch — striking e5 at once to open the center and free the pieces for quick, active development.
notes.teaches: The Scotch opens the center immediately with d4.

notes.explains: Bishop to c4 trains on f7 — the softest square in Black's camp — building long-term pressure and setting up sacrificial ideas against the king.
notes.teaches: Place the bishop on c4 to pressure f7 and prepare tactics.

notes.explains: e5 is a decoy thrust — it attacks the knight on f6 and, if Black grabs it, opens lines to spring Bxf7-based tactics against the king.
notes.teaches: A central pawn push can act as a decoy, luring pieces away and opening attacking lines.

notes.explains: White occupies the centre with the pawn to d4 — the sound, measured way to meet the Alekhine, building the big centre without overreaching.
notes.teaches: Against the Alekhine's provocation, occupy the centre soundly rather than lunging forward.
notes.plans: Complete the centre, then develop.

notes.explains: Recapture with the c-pawn — the recommended choice. It teaches you to play with an imbalanced structure: White gets a queenside pawn majority, Black a kingside majority, and each side plays where it is stronger.
notes.teaches: Recapturing toward the wing creates majorities — an imbalance you steer for your own plans.
notes.plans: Play on the kingside where your majority lies.

notes.explains: The pawn to g6 prepares the fianchetto. The light-squared bishop has a hard time finding a good diagonal here, so the natural home for the dark-squared bishop is the long diagonal on g7.
notes.teaches: When a bishop's natural diagonal is blocked, fianchetto it to the long diagonal instead.
notes.plans: Fianchetto, castle, and target the centre.

notes.explains: The knight to c6 completes the plan: Black's pieces bear down on White's two central pawns. That pressure is the whole point of the setup.
notes.teaches: In the Alekhine the target is the pawn centre — pile pieces against it.
notes.plans: Pressure c4 and d4; provoke a concession.

notes.explains: d4 opens the Four Knights into gambit territory — after Black captures, White has the sharp Belgrade in store rather than the quiet main line.
notes.teaches: Use the Four Knights move order to reach a surprise gambit.

notes.explains: Nd5 is the Belgrade Gambit — instead of recapturing on d4, White centralizes the knight, throwing a rare, aggressive problem at Black that's easy to mishandle over the board.
notes.teaches: A well-timed piece leap can be worth a pawn when it creates immediate concrete problems.

notes.explains: The pawn to g6 is one of the two main replies; the other is e6. Players of the Paulsen or Taimanov structures gravitate to e6, while g6 heads for a Dragon-like fianchetto — pick the one that matches your style.
notes.teaches: Meet the Rossolimo with the setup that mirrors the Sicilian structures you already know.
notes.plans: Fianchetto and develop harmoniously.

notes.explains: Instead of the accelerated setup Black answers with the small pawn to d6 — the classical Sicilian move order, a window into how a grandmaster handles the opening he knows best.
notes.teaches: d6 keeps every classical Sicilian structure open — Najdorf, Scheveningen, Dragon — deferring the choice.
notes.plans: Develop flexibly and pick the structure later.

notes.explains: The bishop checks from b5 — the Moscow, or Canal, Variation. Rather than the open Sicilian, White pins toward the king and invites a block.
notes.teaches: The Moscow (Bb5+) sidesteps mainline Sicilian theory by trading or provoking a block on d7.
notes.plans: Choose the block that keeps winning chances.

notes.explains: The knight to d7 is the ambitious block. The bishop to d7 leads to a lot of draws and the queen to d7 to dry positions; the knight strikes the balance — sharp, playing for a win, yet not objectively dubious. It is the choice of top players pressing with Black.
notes.teaches: When choosing how to meet a check, weigh solidity against winning chances — the knight block keeps the game alive.
notes.plans: Develop behind the knight and keep the position rich.

notes.explains: White grabs queenside space with the pawn to a4, a recently fashionable try that clamps down on Black's ...b5 expansion before it can start.
notes.teaches: A rook-pawn thrust like a4 is prophylaxis — it stops the opponent's freeing break in advance.
notes.plans: Ignore it and develop; the break can wait.

notes.explains: The pawn to e6 sets up a Scheveningen structure — the flexible small-centre Sicilian. Black actively welcomes White playing d4, which simply hands over the very structure Black is aiming for.
notes.teaches: The Scheveningen's small pawn centre (d6/e6) is flexible and hard to attack — invite d4 to reach it.
notes.plans: Complete development and meet d4 with the standard recapture.

notes.explains: White obliges with the pawn to d4, and the position becomes exactly the Sicilian structure Black wanted — a familiar open-Sicilian Scheveningen with a slightly better-placed white bishop as the only difference.
notes.teaches: Transposing into a structure you know beats fighting an unfamiliar one, even at a small objective cost.
notes.plans: Recapture, castle, and play the standard plans.

notes.explains: Castling completes development into a clean open-Sicilian Scheveningen. There is no rush for ...a6 — the b5-bishop is not a real nuisance, and the move is saved for the moment it truly counts, the threat stronger than the execution.
notes.teaches: Hold a useful move in reserve — an unforced ...a6 spends a tempo the position may need later.
notes.plans: Finish the setup, keep ...a6 for the right moment.

notes.explains: The queen settles on c7 — the move that completes the standard Sicilian formation. Nothing deep, just good development: the queen is better placed here, eyeing the c-file and supporting the central and queenside breaks.
notes.teaches: Queen to c7 is the natural finishing touch of the Scheveningen — c-file pressure and break support.
notes.plans: Prepare the ...d5 or ...b5 break from a fully developed position.

notes.explains: The traditional response is the pawn to d5. Many Black players are really bluffing White into locking the centre with e5 — but there is no need to oblige, and capturing keeps White better.
notes.teaches: Don't be bluffed into closing the centre; capture and play against the structure.
notes.plans: Take, saddle Black with an isolated d-pawn, and blockade.

notes.explains: The bishop check on b5 gains a tempo, and the plan behind it is clean: capture on c5 to leave Black with an isolated d-pawn, then blockade and pressure it for the rest of the game.
notes.teaches: Use a tempo-gaining check to set up the capture that fixes the opponent's isolani.
notes.plans: Bxc5, blockade d5, and trade toward a better endgame.

notes.explains: d4 challenges the center against the Philidor's ...d6 — opening lines to leave White with the freer, better-developed position.
notes.teaches: Strike with d4 to gain central control against a passive defense.

notes.explains: g3 is the sneaky idea — the bishop fianchettoes to g2, where it clamps down on the d5-square and makes it very hard for Black to free himself with ...d5.
notes.teaches: Fianchetto the light bishop to control d5 and stifle the opponent's freeing break.

notes.explains: Retreating the knight to e2 keeps a grip on d5 and reroutes it toward the fine f4 or d5 outposts, rather than blocking on d4 after ...c5.
notes.teaches: Reroute a knight off an exchange-prone square to keep an outpost under control.

notes.explains: Black meets e4 with the pawn to e6 — the French. The plan today is aggressive: build toward the enemy king and see if the attack can land a checkmate.
notes.teaches: The French invites a fight where White can play for a direct kingside attack.
notes.plans: Clamp the centre and hunt the king.

notes.explains: The pawn goes to e5 — the Advance. This is the Steinitz treatment, a line that has been around forever but flies under the radar: the e5-pawn locks Black in and the whole game will orbit around keeping it there.
notes.teaches: In the Advance French, the e5-pawn is the clamp — everything supports it.
notes.plans: Advance e5 and build around the clamp.

notes.explains: Black strikes with the pawn to c5, and here everyone and their brother plays c3 to shore up d4. Not today — giving that pawn away looks unthinkable, and that's exactly the point of the line.
notes.teaches: The gambit idea: don't reflexively defend d4 — the initiative can be worth the pawn.
notes.plans: Ignore c5, keep developing.

notes.explains: Pretend nothing is happening and develop the knight to f3. The d4-pawn can fall; what matters is the e5-pawn and a fast, harmonious setup behind it.
notes.teaches: Prioritise the clamping pawn and development over a materially even but passive c3.
notes.plans: Develop; let d4 go if it must.

notes.explains: Bishop to d3, still developing as if the centre weren't on fire — and quietly inviting Black to grab the pawn. Let him: the e5-pawn is the one really squeezing his position, so that's the pawn to nurse.
notes.teaches: Trade a defended pawn's tension for lead in development; keep the pawn that cramps the opponent.
notes.plans: Bd3, castle, overprotect e5.

notes.explains: Castle and accelerate — the rook is coming to e1 not to attack yet but to over-protect e5. Leave d4 alone, pile support behind the clamp, and let development do the talking.
notes.teaches: Over-protection: heap defenders on your key pawn so it can never be undermined.
notes.plans: O-O, Re1, keep e5 bulletproof.

notes.explains: The knight to h6 is the standard French rerouting — it's heading for f5. Don't capture it; taking only helps Black's structure and hands him the open lines he wants.
notes.teaches: Don't grab a knight bound for a good square if the recapture repairs the opponent's position.
notes.plans: Leave the knight, keep developing.

notes.explains: The knight to c3 — looking deeper, this stops the ...Nb4-d6 idea that would dig at the light bishop, and it develops toward the centre. Sometimes the useful move is simply the one that denies the opponent his plan.
notes.teaches: A developing move that also prevents the opponent's regrouping is doubly valuable.
notes.plans: Nc3, deny ...Nb4-d6.

notes.explains: Here is the move to burn into memory: with a knight on c3 and the enemy queen on b6, always look at the knight to a4. It hits the queen and the c5-pawn at once, and Black's whole queenside starts to wobble.
notes.teaches: Nc3 + enemy queen on b6 is a standing cue: Na4 forks the queen and c5.
notes.plans: Na4, win the tempo and the c5 tension.

notes.explains: The knight takes on c5 and the bishop recaptures — and that's the real gain. When the dust settles Black's dark-squared bishop has been traded off, White owns the two bishops, and Black's position is positionally in shambles.
notes.teaches: Trading a knight to eliminate a key bishop can be a positional win — the bishop pair is the prize.
notes.plans: Win the bishop pair, then press.

notes.explains: No rush to attack — the pawn to c3 guards the d4-square, a very typical, solid touch, and Black's ...Ng4 is nothing to fear because the queen to e2 and a later h3 simply shove it back. Play it positionally first.
notes.teaches: Consolidate a key square before attacking; a harmless knight sortie is met by kicking it away.
notes.plans: c3, Be3, complete development.

notes.explains: The pawn to b4 isn't just a hit on the queen — it stakes out c5 as an outpost. Every tempo now buys an important square for the pieces, and the bishop already has its eye on that hole.
notes.teaches: Gain a tempo AND a square in one move — attacking with purpose, not just for the check.
notes.plans: b4, claim the c5 outpost.

notes.explains: The bishop swings to d6, parking itself right in Black's gut and slicing down the diagonal. There was no hurry — but with everything else in place, planting it here is a fine way to finish the buildup.
notes.teaches: Post a bishop on a dominant central square once the rest of the setup is complete.
notes.plans: Bd6, then switch to the kingside.

notes.explains: Now for the concrete phase. Development is done, the bishop dominates, and Black's king is stuck in the centre with no castling in sight — so the knight jumps to g5 and the queen heads for h5. This is going for the throat.
notes.teaches: Only launch the direct attack once development is complete and the enemy king is fixed.
notes.plans: Ng5, Qh5, mate the stranded king.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian, Black strikes with c5, challenging White's centre and opening lines for the fianchettoed bishop — refusing to sit passively against White's quiet setup.
notes.teaches: Meet a slow White system by striking the centre with c5.
notes.plans: Follow with Qa5 pressure and watch the c3-knight.

notes.explains: The queen to a5 loads pressure onto the knight on c3, and it sets a trap: if White ever loosens his grip on c3, the fianchetto bishop and the queen combine to win material there.
notes.teaches: Pile the queen onto a knight the fianchetto bishop also eyes — the pressure turns tactical.

notes.explains: The tactic springs: after the knights come off, the bishop takes on c3 with check and the queen recaptures with check too, forking the king and the loose rook on a1. White's position collapses.
notes.teaches: A bishop-then-queen capture on c3 with check can fork the king and the corner rook.

notes.explains: The pawn to c3 builds the chain, so the bishop on g7 is biting on granite — it stares at d4 but can't budge it. The one downside is that c3 denies the knight its natural c3-square; no problem, the knight simply develops to d2 instead.
notes.teaches: c3 blunts the fianchetto and hands the b1-knight a d2 route instead of c3.
notes.plans: c3, then Nbd2.

notes.explains: Just like in the London, once you've built the little pawn house you put the bishop in its hole — the bishop to d3. Try to get the dark-squared pieces sorted before that knight commits, and otherwise just develop naturally.
notes.teaches: Slot the bishop into the pawn-chain's hole and develop by principle.
notes.plans: Bd3, then complete development.

notes.explains: Black plays the pawn to d5, and closing with e5 is a no-brainer. The move to g6 already weakened all the dark squares, and shutting the centre makes those squares far easier to target — this becomes a French-style Advance with an extra hole on f6.
notes.teaches: Close the centre to fix the opponent's dark-square weaknesses in place.
notes.plans: e5, then play on the dark squares.

notes.explains: When Black locks it further with the pawn to c4, that suits White perfectly — the queenside is sealed, the d4-pawn is under no real pressure, and White gets what amounts to a free hand to attack on the kingside.
notes.teaches: A closed queenside frees you to throw everything at the other wing.
notes.plans: Ignore c4, attack the kingside.

notes.explains: The attack will aim at the dark squares Black conceded — above all f6 and e5. The job now is to route the b1-knight toward those holes, and everything is arranged around getting it there.
notes.teaches: Plan a knight tour toward the opponent's key dark-square holes.
notes.plans: Maneuver the knight to f6/e5.

notes.explains: The rook to e1 looks odd, even bad — but its purpose is to vacate f1 for the knight. The route is knight to d2, to f1, then to e3 or g4, and on toward the f6-square.
notes.teaches: A quiet rook move can clear a path for a knight maneuver — look past the surface.
notes.plans: Re1, then Nd2-f1-e3.

notes.explains: The knight came to f5, and the bishop to g5 exploits its drawback: it hits the queen with tempo along the now-open diagonal, keeps the clamp on f6, and readies the pawn to g4 to chase the knight.
notes.teaches: Punish a knight sortie by developing with tempo while maintaining your grip on the key square.
notes.plans: Bg5, then g4 to harass.

notes.explains: Black's pawn to f6 does White's work: after the trades the e5-square becomes a gaping weakness. Occupy it with a knight, not a rook — a rook is a poor blockader — and there's no rush to do it.
notes.teaches: When the opponent trades off a defender, the vacated square is a permanent outpost; garrison it with a knight.
notes.plans: Aim a knight at e5.

notes.explains: The knight to e3 keeps to the plan, eyeing g4 and then the e5-outpost. Flexible, unhurried — the square isn't going anywhere.
notes.teaches: Reroute the knight step by step toward the outpost; flexibility beats haste.
notes.plans: Ne3-g4, then e5.

notes.explains: With total control of e5 there's no need to rush a piece onto it — nobody can contest it. Connect the rooks first, maybe double on the e-file, and stay patient; here the threat is stronger than the execution.
notes.teaches: When you own a square, improve elsewhere first — the threat to occupy it is often worth more than occupying it.
notes.plans: Connect rooks, keep e5 in reserve.

notes.explains: Before anything else, stop Black's one idea — the pawn to g5. The move to h4 does it; f4 would only weaken things by cutting the queen's diagonal. The h4 and g3 arrangement locks the kingside down.
notes.teaches: Prevent the opponent's only break; choose the restraining pawn move that doesn't weaken your own position.
notes.plans: h4 (not f4), then g3.

notes.explains: Normally you'd keep the knight on e5, but concretely the capture on g4 transforms the advantage — the knight has done its job, and now the rook simply collects the pawn on e6, leaving White up material with that monster e5-square intact.
notes.teaches: Trade a dominating piece when the concrete line converts the positional edge into material.
notes.plans: Nxg4, then Rxe6.

notes.explains: Don't reflexively retreat the rook — marinate on the position and remember the bishop kept on c2 all game. It rakes the diagonal toward h7, and that's why the rook can crash into g6 with decisive threats. Black resigns.
notes.teaches: A quietly preserved bishop can be the piece that finishes — don't forget your long-diagonal attacker.
notes.plans: Rxg6 with the Bc2 battery.

notes.explains: d4 opens the Danish Gambit — White offers pawns to blow the center open and generate a raging development lead.
notes.teaches: Gambit central pawns to accelerate development and open lines.

notes.explains: Bishop to c4 completes the Danish — with two pawns sacrificed, the bishops rake toward f7 and the whole army will crash out with tempo.
notes.teaches: In the Danish, aim the bishops at f7 and prize activity over the two pawns.

notes.explains: Recapturing on c3 with the knight leaves White a massive lead in development and open lines — the two pawns are gone, but Black is badly behind and cramped.
notes.teaches: Measure a gambit by development and activity, not the pawn count.

notes.explains: d5 is the critical counter — meeting White's flank gambit with a strike in the center, the classic antidote to a wing pawn advance.
notes.teaches: Answer a flank attack with a central counterstrike.

notes.explains: Knight takes on e4 regains the gambit pawn and keeps the knight boldly centralized — Black already stands comfortably, with a healthy share of the center.
notes.teaches: Recapture to a strong central square, equalizing material with an active piece.

notes.explains: Bishop to c5 develops with bite — it eyes f2, the tender square in White's camp, while Black keeps the strong knight parked on e4.
notes.teaches: Develop actively toward f2 while keeping your centralized pieces in place.

notes.explains: The move b5 grabs queenside space and kicks the bishop back — a useful insertion that removes the Bxc6 ideas before Black commits to the freeing ...d5 plan.
notes.teaches: Insert a useful tempo-gaining pawn move before your main freeing break.

notes.explains: d5 is the Marshall Gambit — Black boldly sacrifices the e5-pawn to blow the center open and unleash a ferocious attack on White's king, buying the initiative for a pawn.
notes.teaches: Sacrifice a central pawn to open lines and seize a lasting attacking initiative.

notes.explains: Queen to h4 hurls the last attacker at the white king — the standard Marshall follow-up, coordinating queen, bishop and knight for threats on the kingside.
notes.teaches: Bring the queen into the attack to combine with your active pieces against the king.

notes.explains: c6 is a provocative waiting move against the King's Gambit — it holds ...d5 back for one move, luring White to commit before Black strikes the center.
notes.teaches: A quiet waiting move can provoke the opponent into a committal setup before you counter.

notes.explains: Now d5 strikes the center — with White's knight already on f3, this counter hits e4 and prepares to seize a dominant pawn front.
notes.teaches: Time the central ...d5 break to hit the opponent's pawns once their pieces are committed.

notes.explains: e4 is the key thrust — it drives the knight from f3, and after Black recovers the pawn he owns a huge, dominating center while White's king sits exposed.
notes.teaches: Gain tempo by attacking a knight with a pawn, then convert the space into a strong center.

notes.explains: The knight retreats to g6, sidestepping the sharpest lines of the Halloween Gambit — Black is up a piece and simply needs to weather White's pawn advances.
notes.teaches: When accepting a gambit, dodge the opponent's prepared theory and consolidate the extra material.

notes.explains: Rather than fussing over the attacked knight, Black develops with Bb4 — pinning the knight on c3 and calmly bringing pieces out while a piece up.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, keep developing and let the opponent's threats resolve themselves.

notes.explains: Recapturing with the queen on f6 leaves Black comfortably a piece up with a healthy structure — the Halloween Gambit has fizzled out.
notes.teaches: Once you've consolidated, a gambit accepted simply leaves you ahead in material.

notes.explains: Against the delayed Alapin the accurate move is the knight to f6, hitting the e4-pawn and forcing White to make a decision about the centre right away.
notes.teaches: Meet the delayed Alapin with Nf6, pressing e4 and provoking a commitment.
notes.plans: Develop actively and target the centre.

notes.explains: White's push to e5 is simply not good — Black captures on e5 and stands at least equal, since the advance loosens White's centre without any concrete gain.
notes.teaches: An unprepared e5 push just drops the tension in Black's favour — take it and equalise.
notes.plans: Capture on e5 and develop with a free hand.

notes.explains: The knight to d7 is the efficient path — challenging the advanced e5-knight while developing. It keeps Black's structure clean and the pieces active.
notes.teaches: Develop while questioning the opponent's advanced piece — one move, two jobs.
notes.plans: Challenge e5, complete development, and take over.

notes.explains: Black's c5 is the trap-trigger. With the bishop on c4 raking toward f7 and the king still in the centre, loosening the queenside like this invites a tactic — the alarm bells should ring the moment that bishop appears on c4.
notes.teaches: When the enemy bishop eyes f7 and your king is uncastled, a loosening pawn move can walk into tactics.

notes.explains: White punishes with the check on b5. It drags a piece to d7 and clears the way for the knight to jump to f5 and b5, unravelling Black's position with tempo.
notes.teaches: Refute a loosening move with a forcing check that pries open tactical lines.

notes.explains: The pawn to f3 is the Fantasy — the kryptonite of many Caro players: less studied, sharply tactical, and it forces Black to know real theory instead of drifting.
notes.teaches: An offbeat but sound line forces the opponent out of memorized moves.

notes.explains: The bishop to c4 fixes on f7. The sacrifice on f7 becomes a standing threat for the whole middlegame, so Black can never fully relax there.
notes.teaches: Keep a live sacrificial threat on f7 to restrict the defender's freedom.
notes.plans: Castle and pile toward f7.

notes.explains: The bishop can't just sit, so it travels: to g5, and when kicked it retreats along h4 to g3 — each step provoking a pawn move, first h6 then g5, that permanently weakens Black's kingside.
notes.teaches: A repositioning bishop can provoke weakening pawn pushes as it travels.

notes.explains: Black's instinct in the King's Indian: strike the centre fast. The pawn to c5 hits d4 at once, and if White grabs it Black will round it back up with tempo while developing.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, challenge the centre quickly — a temporary pawn is worth fast development.
notes.plans: Na6 and Qa5 to regain c5 with initiative.

notes.explains: Knight to a6 and queen to a5 come as a pair, both eyeing the loose c5-pawn and the knight on c3 — pressure that also develops. The aim is initiative, not merely the pawn.
notes.teaches: Coordinate Na6 and Qa5 to hit c5 and c3 with tempo.

notes.explains: The knight to e4 is the shot that nearly wins on the spot. Combined with the queen on a5 and the knight on a6, it strains White's position past the point where everything can be held.
notes.teaches: An active knight leap to e4 turns positional pressure into a concrete threat.

notes.explains: Black cashes the pressure in, winning the dark-squared bishop to claim the bishop pair — the payoff of a model King's Indian squeeze where fast development simply outran White's loose setup.
notes.teaches: Convert accumulated pressure into a lasting trump like the bishop pair.

notes.explains: White offers the Smith-Morra Gambit with the pawn to c3, hoping Black grabs the pawn and lets him develop with a lead. Against it there's a practical, rarely-seen answer coming — one good enough to win a strong Titled Tuesday game.
notes.teaches: The Smith-Morra trades a pawn for development; a rare declining line can sidestep all White's prep.
notes.plans: Decline the gambit, keep it solid.

notes.explains: The natural reaction is the knight to f6, developing and steering away from a queen trade. Keeping the queens on suits the side that's better developed, and Black is happy to keep pieces on the board.
notes.teaches: Develop with ...Nf6 and avoid the queen trade when you hold the initiative.
notes.plans: ...Nf6, then ...Nc6 with tempo.

notes.explains: The knight to c6 hits the queen with tempo, and now precision is required. Don't leap the knight into e4 — the pawn to f3 would trap it. The clean move is the knight back to d7: it concedes the d5-pawn but keeps everything safe and coordinated.
notes.teaches: Watch for the trap: an active-looking knight to e4 gets caught by f3 — retreat to d7 instead.
notes.plans: ...Nd7, stay solid, keep the edge.

notes.explains: From here it's easy conversion. The pawn to b5 kicks the bishop and Black simply grabs the central pawn, then hurries the pieces out. When you're up material, speed of development finishes the job.
notes.teaches: Convert a material edge by grabbing loose pawns and developing quickly — no heroics needed.
notes.plans: ...b5, win the pawn, develop.

notes.explains: The knight to c4 centralises, heading for its best square. Improving the worst-placed piece is the quiet engine of conversion.
notes.teaches: Centralise your pieces while ahead; a knight on c4 dominates.
notes.plans: ...Nc4, improve every piece.

notes.explains: Here's the whole roadmap: develop your pieces to active squares — the rook to c8 — then identify the biggest target and trade pieces when it doesn't harm your position. Simple, methodical, and decisive when you're already better.
notes.teaches: Conversion roadmap: activate pieces, name the target, trade favourably.
notes.plans: ...Rc8, target c3, simplify.

notes.explains: The knight to e4 hits the pawn and invites White to trade off his well-placed knight on e5. Encouraging the exchange of the opponent's best piece is exactly how you loosen a position.
notes.teaches: Provoke the trade of the opponent's most active piece to remove his last source of play.
notes.plans: ...Ne4, trade off the e5-knight.

notes.explains: And now the tactical eye earns its keep. The pawn on c3 is the standing target, but there's a sharper idea: whenever White has pushed the f-pawn with the king on g1, tactics along the a7-g1 diagonal are in the air. The knight to g4 is the shot that cashes in.
notes.teaches: With White's f-pawn advanced and king on g1, hunt for tactics on the a7-g1 diagonal.
notes.plans: ...Ng4, strike on the diagonal.

notes.explains: With the pawn on g6 Black clears the way to fianchetto the bishop to g7, where it will rake the long diagonal from the corner straight through the centre toward White's queenside.
notes.teaches: In the Dragon the dark-squared bishop is the star piece — the whole setup is built around its diagonal.
notes.plans: Fianchetto the bishop to g7, castle, and lean on the centre from afar.

notes.explains: The bishop settles on g7 and immediately leans on the long diagonal; its first target is the knight on d4, the piece holding White's grip on the centre.
notes.teaches: A fianchettoed bishop fights for the centre from a distance — contesting d4 is the Dragon's opening battle.
notes.plans: Castle, then pile onto d4 and the half-open c-file.

notes.explains: The bishop backs up the d4-knight and readies castling long — the sharp opposite-wings main line. Capturing on c6 instead would be a concession: Black recaptures toward the centre and the b-file opens against b2.
notes.teaches: Trading the knight on c6 hands Black the open b-file and an easy central break — so White keeps the tension.
notes.plans: Both sides head for opposite-side castling and a race.

notes.explains: This is what keeps it an ACCELERATED Dragon: the knight comes to f6 before the d-pawn commits. Play the pawn to d6 now and White gets f3, transposing into a Main-Line Dragon; holding the pawn on its home square keeps the one-move central break in reserve.
notes.teaches: Move order is the Accelerated Dragon's whole point — delay the small pawn push so the full central break in a single move stays available.
notes.plans: Keep the d-pawn home; aim to strike the centre in one move later.

notes.explains: A rule to burn in: once White's queen leaves its home square in a Dragon, look hard at the knight leap to g4. Trading that knight for the dark-squared bishop leaves the g7-bishop without a rival on its diagonal. The catch — after the leap the bishop can't step off e3, since the twice-attacked d4-knight would fall, so White's only try is to capture on c6 first.
notes.teaches: Prise off White's dark-squared bishop and your g7-bishop rules the long diagonal uncontested.
notes.plans: Castle, keep the g4-leap in reserve, and watch the d-file.

notes.explains: With the concrete lines still murky, the soundest choice is to finish developing and castle. The pawn deliberately stays home: if White insists on a Main-Line Dragon setup, the central break in one move is the reward.
notes.teaches: When the calculation is unclear, complete development before forcing matters.
notes.plans: King to safety, pieces ready, break the centre when it counts.

notes.explains: White castles long, and now the king and queen sit on the same file — that changes the whole assessment. The knight leap to g4 comes back on: after the capture on c6 and the bishop's move to d4, the bishop swings to h6 and pins the queen to the king. White blocks with f4, but then the e-pawn hits f4 and, with the pin freezing it, wins material.
notes.teaches: A move that failed a moment ago can work once the pieces shift — recalculate the instant the position changes.
notes.plans: Play the knight to g4 now, heading for the h6-pin.

notes.explains: The knight jumps in with a double point: it eyes the bishop on e3 and, with the queen no longer home, the whole h6-pin idea is live. The bishop still can't move — the d4-knight is attacked twice and would drop.
notes.teaches: A knight on g4 both harasses the e3-bishop and clears the g7-bishop's diagonal.
notes.plans: Provoke the capture on c6, then swing the bishop to h6.

notes.explains: Recapturing toward the centre swings the b-file wide open, and with White castled long that file points straight at b2 — the attack writes itself. The c-pawn now becomes a battering ram against White's king cover.
notes.teaches: Recapture toward the centre to open a file; against a queenside-castled king the half-open b-file is gold.
notes.plans: Queen to b6 or a5, rook to b8, and prise open b2.

notes.explains: There it is — the bishop swings to h6 and pins the queen to the king along the dark diagonal. The queen is nailed in place.
notes.teaches: With White's king on c1 and queen on d2, the h6-to-c1 diagonal is a pin waiting to happen.
notes.plans: Meet the block f4 with the pawn break e5.

notes.explains: The crusher. The e-pawn strikes f4, and because the queen is pinned the pawn cannot capture back — it is as if f4 were not there — so the bishop on d4 falls and Black emerges a full piece up. Precision first, though: snatching with the bishop on f4 with check is the tempting error; after the king steps aside, taking on d4 lets White recapture and the f4-bishop is left hanging. Take on d4 first — the f4-pawn is not going anywhere.
notes.teaches: The power of a pin is that the pinned piece cannot defend — a frozen pawn effectively does not exist.
notes.plans: Collect on d4, keep the pin, and convert the extra piece.

notes.explains: White's c4 is the Panov, the most testing weapon against the Caro. It aims for an isolated d-pawn, trading a long-term weakness for active pieces — so Black's task is to blunt that activity and target the d4-pawn.
notes.teaches: Against the Panov, blockade and pressure the isolated d-pawn rather than fear White's early initiative.

notes.explains: The bishop to e6 looks odd — it blocks the f8-bishop — but it over-protects d5, the square the whole isolated-pawn fight revolves around. If White trades on f6, the e-pawn recaptures and the dark-squared bishop's diagonal opens anyway.
notes.teaches: Bolster the key blockade square even with an awkward-looking move; the temporary block resolves itself.

notes.explains: Recapturing on f6 with the e-pawn hands Black the half-open e-file and a clear diagonal for the dark-squared bishop. The doubled f-pawns are a small price for that activity.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are worth accepting when the recapture opens a file and frees a bishop.

notes.explains: The pawn to f5 completes the regrouping: the fianchettoed bishop on g7 now stares down the long diagonal at d4, and Black's patient plan of bishop to g7, castle, then f5 has come off cleanly.
notes.teaches: A clear multi-move plan is worth executing step by step — here fianchetto, castle, then f5 to open the bishop's diagonal.
notes.plans: Press the d4-pawn down the long diagonal.

notes.explains: The bishop check on b5 is the point of this whole system against the Nf6 Scandinavian — it provokes a block, and the natural blocks leave Black slightly awkward.
notes.teaches: A check that forces a clumsy block is worth a tempo — the b5 bishop unbalances Black's development.
notes.plans: Retreat the bishop and keep the small pull.

notes.explains: White tries the gambit move order — the pawn to c3, offering the Smith-Morra. There is no need to grab it and play into White's development lead.
notes.teaches: You don't have to accept a gambit — a sound decline can sidestep the attacker's whole idea.
notes.plans: Decline by transposing to a structure you know.

notes.explains: The knight to f6 is the antidote: it declines the Morra and transposes straight into an Alapin structure, where White has no dangerous gambit — just an ordinary position.
notes.teaches: Nf6 here converts the Smith-Morra into a harmless Alapin — refute the gambit by transposition.
notes.plans: Reach the familiar Alapin and equalise comfortably.

notes.explains: After the pawn to e5 and the knight to d5, the position is a normal Alapin Sicilian — comfortable and low-risk for Black, with none of the Morra's initiative to fear.
notes.teaches: Steer a gambit into a quiet known structure and the attacking chances evaporate.
notes.plans: Develop soundly; no gambit pressure remains.

notes.explains: The pawn to c5 arrives and the normal move would be c3 — but not here. The knight to f3, leaving d4, is the treatment: an idea of Nimzowitsch's whose whole purpose is to accelerate White's development.
notes.teaches: Nf3 over c3: give the pawn, take the lead in development.
notes.plans: Develop fast, fight for e5.

notes.explains: Develop as if nothing is happening — the bishop to d3, not b5. The bishop to b5 is a very common mistake in these positions: the queenside pin is rarely dangerous, whereas from d3 the bishop points straight at the kingside where Black will castle.
notes.teaches: Prefer Bd3 aiming at the king over the tempting but toothless ...Bb5 pin.
notes.plans: Bd3, castle, target the king.

notes.explains: Now the zen of the whole system: establish total control of the e5-square. That advanced pawn — and the piece that replaces it — is everything. Lose the grip on e5 and Black's pawns start rolling up the board; hold it and Black stays cramped.
notes.teaches: The system lives or dies on control of e5 — a pawn there can be replaced by a piece, but never relinquish the square.
notes.plans: Pile defenders on e5.

notes.explains: So the rook comes to e1, reinforcing the e5-point before Black can chip at it. Rook to e1 or bishop to f4 — either adds a guard to the square the whole game revolves around.
notes.teaches: Add defenders to your key square proactively, before it's attacked.
notes.plans: Re1 to back up e5.

notes.explains: Recapturing with the knight on e5 keeps the grip — the pawn is gone but a piece takes its place, and control of the square is unbroken.
notes.teaches: A piece can inherit a pawn's outpost; the square matters more than which unit holds it.
notes.plans: Nxe5, keep the clamp.

notes.explains: The bishop goes to f4, and don't be seduced by the one-move pin on g5. The goal isn't a cheap pin — it's more control of e5. Even if f4 looks a touch lame, positionally it's the right call because it guards the square.
notes.teaches: Choose the move that serves your strategic goal over a flashy one-move pin.
notes.plans: Bf4, reinforce e5.

notes.explains: Even more control is needed, so combine two jobs in one: develop the last knight to a square where it heads for f3 and adds yet another defender of e5. Bring the undeveloped piece out and let it reinforce the battle square at the same time.
notes.teaches: Develop a piece toward the exact square it can also defend — economy of tempo.
notes.plans: Nd2 then Ndf3, stacking guards on e5.

notes.explains: With the knight to f3 there are now so many pieces holding e5 that any single one can leave its post and the square still stands — that was the whole point. Just stay alert to the x-ray on the undefended bishop; a later drop back to g3 is the tidy prophylactic.
notes.teaches: Over-guard a square so no single trade or departure loosens it; watch for x-ray discoveries.
notes.plans: Ndf3; keep Bg3 in reserve.

notes.explains: The capture on c6 comes with force — the recapture with the b-pawn is forced, because otherwise the queen simply hangs. That opens the way to collect on d6 next.
notes.teaches: A capture that also attacks the queen forces the recapture — read the in-between threat.
notes.plans: Nxc6, then win on d6.

notes.explains: A textbook never-pre-move moment: the rook takes on c4 looks great, but calculate one move further — Black replies c5 and rips open a massive diagonal for the bishop, and White isn't better. Take the two seconds; the right move is the queen to d4.
notes.teaches: Never pre-move a natural recapture — check one move deeper for the opponent's resource.
notes.plans: Qxd4, not the hasty Rxc4.

notes.explains: The queen to d4 hits the enemy queen, and a trade there leaves Black's pawn structure in ruins. This is the typical way to convert: force the queens off into a position where the static weaknesses decide.
notes.teaches: Offer a queen trade that leaves the opponent with a wrecked structure.
notes.plans: Qxd4, trade into a better ending.

notes.explains: The pawn to e6 is a third-tier move — respectable but a notch below the main d5 and Nf6. Its interesting property is transpositional: after d4 it can funnel into the same structures as the main lines.
notes.teaches: A sideline that transposes into your main lines is nothing to fear — steer it home.
notes.plans: Play d4 and reach a familiar structure.

notes.explains: The bishop jumps to c4, hitting the knight — but this is the Alekhine's game. The knight retreats to b6, its ideal square, and the bishop must move again, having gained nothing.
notes.teaches: In the Alekhine the knight belongs on b6 — let it be chased there and the attacker loses time.
notes.plans: Retreat to b6, then strike the centre.

notes.explains: The bishop drops back to e2, a passive post — and that is the signal to press. White has spent moves shuffling the bishop while building no real centre.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces retreat without a plan, seize the initiative.
notes.plans: Challenge the centre before White consolidates.

notes.explains: The most accurate move is the pawn to d6, striking at the e5-pawn. The knight to c6 is playable, but with White holding so little of the centre there is no reason not to challenge it directly.
notes.teaches: Attack an overextended centre at once rather than developing around it.
notes.plans: Trade on e5 and expose the weakness.

notes.explains: Take on e5 and steer for the trade of queens. If White recaptures on the knight, the knight takes d4 and wins; and once the queens come off, the pawn on e5 becomes a huge, permanent weakness — the whole point of the Alekhine laid bare.
notes.teaches: The Alekhine's payoff: provoke the big centre, trade down, and target the overextended pawn.
notes.plans: Trade queens, then win or tie White to the e5-pawn.

notes.explains: A key restraint: do NOT simply grab on f3 and then take e5 — that drops the b7-pawn. Making the pawn a lasting weakness and tying White to its defence is often stronger than winning it outright and freeing White's pieces.
notes.teaches: A fixed weakness you pressure can be worth more than the pawn itself — restraint over greed.
notes.plans: Pile on e5; don't release the tension prematurely.

notes.explains: Now the pawn on e5 falls to the knight — the pressure converts to material cleanly, with White's pieces still tangled.
notes.teaches: Once the defender is overloaded, collect the weakness you've been pressing.
notes.plans: Bank the pawn and complete development.

notes.explains: The pawn to e6 comes at the right moment — earlier it would have locked the light-squared bishop behind the pawns; now it opens the bishop's path out.
notes.teaches: Time the freeing pawn move so it releases your bishop rather than entombing it.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop and convert the extra pawn.

notes.explains: The pawn to c3 — the Alapin. Instead of a theory-heavy Open Sicilian, White prepares to build a big centre with d4 and simply gets a pleasant, better position out of the opening again and again.
notes.teaches: The Alapin sidesteps Sicilian theory and fights for a classical pawn centre.
notes.plans: Follow with d4 and occupy the centre.

notes.explains: After the centre is exchanged, Black essentially must play d5 to get a viable game — every other move hands White full control of the centre and a wonderful position.
notes.teaches: In the Alapin, if Black doesn't hit back with d5, White simply owns the centre.
notes.plans: If Black doesn't play d5, seize the centre with pieces.

notes.explains: The pawn to d6 is a common inaccuracy — it declines the d5 break and cedes the centre. White is already better and can develop with a free hand.
notes.teaches: Passing up the freeing break in the Alapin is a real, if quiet, concession.
notes.plans: Build the centre and develop with tempo.

notes.explains: Develop the knight to c3 first, not f3 — the knight on f3 would allow the pin with the bishop on g4. There is no reason to hand Black that extra option.
notes.teaches: Choose the developing move that denies the opponent a useful pin.
notes.plans: Restrict the c8-bishop before committing the king's knight.

notes.explains: The little pawn to h3 restricts the light-squared bishop, taking g4 away and nudging it toward the far more passive d7-square. A small move with a lasting positional point.
notes.teaches: A timely h3 denies the bishop its active diagonal and keeps it passive.
notes.plans: Complete development behind the big centre.

notes.explains: Place the bishop on d3, NOT c4. On c4 it would be vulnerable to the pawn thrust b5 and to being hit by the pieces; on d3 it reinforces the centre and stays safe, giving White a free hand on both wings.
notes.teaches: Develop the bishop where it supports the centre and dodges b5 — d3 over c4 here.
notes.plans: Castle, keep the centre, and play on both sides.

notes.explains: Recapturing with the e-pawn defines the Tartakower: Black takes on doubled f-pawns to blast open the e-file and hand the dark-squared bishop a clear diagonal and effortless development.
notes.teaches: Doubled f-pawns are a fair trade for the open e-file and free, harmonious piece play.
notes.plans: Develop actively, castle, and work the open e-file.

notes.explains: The bishop to g4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen behind it — a standard way to build pressure once White has committed the king.
notes.teaches: Pin the defender to develop with a threat instead of a quiet move.

notes.explains: The recapture leaves Black with a solid pawn cube on the kingside — f6, f7, g6, g7 — a compact mass that shields the king while Black plays on the open files.
notes.teaches: A doubled-pawn cluster can be a sturdy defensive cube, not just a weakness.

notes.explains: The pressure cashes in: taking on e3 exploits an overload — the pawn on f2 is guarding two squares at once and cannot hold both, so material falls.
notes.teaches: An overloaded defender guarding two points collapses the moment you strike one of them.

notes.explains: White pushes e5, locking the centre and handing Black an ideal French-style structure — but a French where the light-squared bishop is not yet shut in. The advanced pawn can be undermined at leisure.
notes.teaches: When White locks the centre with e5, get the light bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain before playing e6.

notes.explains: The bishop comes out to f5 before e6 would ever trap it — the one problem piece of the French, solved for free. Black already has an easy, comfortable game against the e5-pawn.
notes.teaches: Developing the light-squared bishop to f5 before e6 is Black's whole edge in these Advance structures.
notes.plans: Play e6, finish developing, and pile onto d4 and e5.

notes.explains: The pawn to f6 strikes at the head of White's chain, prising open the centre and the f-file to get at the d4- and e5-pawns Black has been pressuring.
notes.teaches: Break a cramping pawn chain at its head with f6 to open lines onto its base.

notes.explains: The pawn to f3, the Fantasy again — a line with a shoddy reputation that is genuinely dangerous once you know it.
notes.teaches: f3 keeps the centre and invites the sharp, less-charted play Black often mishandles.

notes.explains: Black's early h5 neglects the centre, so White strikes with e5. The knight on f6 has no good square and is shoved back to the miserable h7, leaving White a huge space edge.
notes.teaches: Punish a flank move that ignores the centre by grabbing space with e5.

notes.explains: White lays a trap: the move h3 quietly offers a central pawn as bait. Black bites — the bishop trades on f3, the queen recaptures, and then wins the pawn, its queen now planted on d4. The bishop to e3 springs the trap, hemming the queen in with tempo where every escape loses.
notes.teaches: Bait a pawn grab and trap the greedy queen by attacking it with a gain of tempo.

notes.explains: Up a queen, White drives home the theme: the weak d6-square. A rook plants itself on d6, using the outpost the e5-pawn created, and Black's position folds.
notes.teaches: An advanced outpost like d6 is a permanent home for a piece — here a rook the pawn on e5 protects.

notes.explains: The French again, and against it the plan is the Steinitz: the pawn to e5 for the Advance, but instead of the usual c3 to prop up d4, a very odd-looking treatment is coming.
notes.teaches: The Steinitz Advance skips c3 — White leans on the e5-clamp rather than the d4-pawn.
notes.plans: Push e5, develop, ignore d4.

notes.explains: Black hits with the pawn to c5 and now the signature move — the knight to f3, leaving d4 to its fate. It looks strange and it scores heavily: development and the e5-clamp matter more than the pawn.
notes.teaches: Nf3 over c3: trade the d4-pawn's defence for speed and the cramping e5-pawn.
notes.plans: Develop fast behind e5.

notes.explains: Bishop to d3, and the capture on d4 simply doesn't matter. The whole idea is to keep developing and let the e5-pawn do the cramping while Black spends moves on a pawn that was never the point.
notes.teaches: Meet ...cxd4 with calm development — the initiative outweighs the pawn.
notes.plans: Bd3, then resolve the centre favourably.

notes.explains: Rather than castle, capture on c5. This reaches exactly the pawn structure Black would have got by taking on d4 — except here White never sacrificed the pawn, and the position is already unpleasant for Black.
notes.teaches: dxc5 can reach the same structure as a pawn sac without paying the pawn — take the free version.
notes.plans: dxc5, recapture, keep the extra tempo.

notes.explains: The knight to c3 is the principled, most testing move. Two things frame the position: Black has no dark-squared bishop, so his remaining bishop is the bad one, and the Greek-gift sacrifice on h7 is quietly on the cards the moment Black castles kingside.
notes.teaches: Note the missing dark-squared bishop and a lurking Bxh7+ before choosing where to develop.
notes.plans: Nc3, eye the light squares and the h7 sac.

notes.explains: With the queen on c7, look at where the knight can go. The knight to b5 is thematic — it wants to sink its teeth into d6, the hole in Black's camp.
notes.teaches: Reroute the knight toward a hole the opponent can't cover — here, d6.
notes.plans: Nb5, aiming at the d6 outpost.

notes.explains: The knight to d6 with check, and it's not too late to strike — d6 is uncovered, so the knight jumps in without preparation. After the trade, a monster pawn lands on d6 and Black's position already stinks.
notes.teaches: When the outpost is uncovered, occupy it with tempo before the opponent can defend it.
notes.plans: Nd6+, then a cramping pawn on d6.

notes.explains: First eliminate the knight with the capture on g6 — because bishop to f4 straight away would just hang the bishop. Take, then play bishop f4: it supports the d6-pawn, and with no dark-squared bishop, Black has nothing to challenge it with.
notes.teaches: Remove the defender/attacker first, then occupy the square the recapture no longer contests.
notes.plans: Bxg6, Bf4, cement d6.

notes.explains: Notice the extra point: recapturing wrecks Black's kingside pawns and opens the h-file, and if Black castles short he steps into an attack down it — while, other than the rook on h8, Black has no kingside firepower to make that file cut both ways.
notes.teaches: Opening a file against a king only helps the side with pieces to pour down it.
notes.plans: Damage the kingside, aim rooks at the h-file.

notes.explains: The knight to g5 is prophylaxis and attack in one. Its main job is to stop ...f6 — because then e6 would hang — and at the same time it joins the hunt on Black's king.
notes.teaches: A single knight move can both prevent the opponent's freeing break and attack the king.
notes.plans: Ng5, deny ...f6, build the attack.

notes.explains: Time for the rook lift — the rook to e3, ready to swing to h3 and join the queen against the king. The pieces are all pointing the same way; now they converge.
notes.teaches: Lift a rook along the third rank to add a heavy piece to the kingside attack.
notes.plans: Re3-h3, then bring the queen in.

notes.explains: With the rook lifted, the queen comes to g4 and the threats mount — rook to h3 next, and the mating net tightens. Everything is in place; the attack plays itself.
notes.teaches: Once the pieces are massed, add the queen last and the mate threats appear on their own.
notes.plans: Qg4, Rh3, deliver mate.

notes.explains: The pawn to f3 is the Fantasy Variation — an offbeat, tricky way to keep the full centre and steer for a quick attack. Its reputation is far worse than its bite.
notes.teaches: f3 holds the centre and invites sharp play many Caro players simply don't know.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the bishop on f7 with check. The point is the reply: after the king takes, the knight leaps to e5 with check and forks the king together with the loose bishop on g4 — check first, win the piece next.
notes.teaches: A sacrifice works when the recapture runs into a knight that checks the king and hits a piece in the same move.

notes.explains: Two pawns up, the black king dragged to g8 and stripped bare, White's knight picks off the bishop that had come to g4. This is already winning, straight out of the opening.
notes.teaches: The sacrifice's dividend is material plus a permanently exposed king.

notes.explains: The queen retreats all the way to d8 — the solid, recently popular system. White simply takes the centre with d4 and develops naturally and actively; there is nothing tricky to fear.
notes.teaches: Against a passive queen retreat, occupy the centre and develop with purpose.
notes.plans: d4, natural development, and pressure the space.

notes.explains: The little pawn to h6 is already a mistake — completely unnecessary, a wasted tempo Black cannot afford in an opening where the queen has already been chased. It can be punished by principled play.
notes.teaches: An unforced luft like h6 in the opening is a tempo you can punish directly.
notes.plans: Develop with threats aimed at f7.

notes.explains: Start the punishment with the bishop to c4, aiming straight at the f7-pawn — the eternal soft spot when Black has spent time on the edge instead of developing.
notes.teaches: When Black wastes time, train the pieces on f7 at once.
notes.plans: Add the knight to the f7 attack.

notes.explains: The knight to e5 piles a second attacker onto f7. With Black underdeveloped, the pressure on the weak point becomes overwhelming almost immediately.
notes.teaches: Two pieces on f7 against an undeveloped king is often already decisive.
notes.plans: Break through on f7.

notes.explains: The knight to c3 reaches the standard Open Sicilian tabiya — the classical, richly-theoretical battleground where White fights for the d5-square and central space.
notes.teaches: The Open Sicilian is the main test — both sides play for the d5-square and the initiative.
notes.plans: Develop and pressure d5.

notes.explains: Black's pawn to e5 is premature — and the punishment is the bishop check on b5. After the block, the hole on d5 becomes permanent: even if the knight is chased to a3, White's grip on that outpost is worth the awkwardness.
notes.teaches: Meet an early …e5 in the Open Sicilian with Bb5+ — the d5-hole it creates is a lasting asset.
notes.plans: Trade the defender of d5 and occupy the outpost.

notes.explains: White grabs space with an early e5 — offbeat, and not dangerous. It shoves a pawn deep before a single piece comes out, and that pawn can be challenged at once.
notes.teaches: An early space grab that skips development can be undermined immediately.

notes.explains: The pawn to d6 strikes at the base of the e5-pawn straight away, forcing the trade so White gets no space edge at all.
notes.teaches: Meet a premature advanced pawn by hitting its base and trading it off — the simplest road to equality.

notes.explains: With d5 Black settles into a symmetrical, dry structure, but with an extra tempo in hand — effectively playing the white side of it.
notes.teaches: In a symmetrical position the free tempo is the small edge to nurse.
notes.plans: Develop smoothly and keep the tempo edge.

notes.explains: The knight jumps to e4, the one bid for an imbalance — planted on a strong central square and daring White to resolve the tension instead of drifting into dead symmetry.
notes.teaches: To play for a win from a symmetrical position, seek a small asymmetry — a centralized knight is one.

notes.explains: This is the critical fork in the road. Three or four sound setups exist here; the Four Pawns Attack is the one for the player who wants to punish the Alekhine — little theory to learn, and a real chance to blow Black off the board.
notes.teaches: Pick your weapon by temperament — the Four Pawns is the aggressive, low-theory way to meet the Alekhine.
notes.plans: Build the four-pawn centre and attack.

notes.explains: The knight to c6 is the main line — and here is the pitfall: the natural knight to f3 is a mistake. It walks straight into the capture on d4 followed by the bishop pin on g4, dropping the e5-pawn. Nor does the knight to e2 help — it blocks the bishop.
notes.teaches: In the Four Pawns, Nf3 too early loses e5 to Nxd4 and Bg4 — develop the other pieces first.
notes.plans: Defend e5 another way before committing the king's knight.

notes.explains: The right way to hold e5 without allowing the pin is the bishop to e3. It defends the centre and keeps the king's knight free to come out only once it is safe.
notes.teaches: Defend with a developing move that doesn't create a pin — the bishop to e3 holds the centre.
notes.plans: Develop the queen's knight, then the king's knight.

notes.explains: Only now, with Black's bishop already committed to f5 and the queen's knight developed, is the knight to f3 safe — the g4-pin has lost its bite. Order of development is everything in this line.
notes.teaches: Delay the king's knight until the enemy bishop can no longer pin it profitably.
notes.plans: Complete development and castle.

notes.explains: After the pawn break f6 is met by the capture and recapture, White stands clearly better: superior central control, a backward black pawn on e6, and beautifully placed pieces.
notes.teaches: A premature pawn break against a big centre often just hands you a backward pawn to target.
notes.plans: Pile up on the backward e6-pawn and the centre.

notes.explains: The knight to e4 aims to trade off the f6-bishop. Once that bishop is gone, the d4-pawn is no longer under pressure and White's pieces are freed from defending the centre. Note the restraint: recapturing on f3 with the bishop would hang the c4-pawn, so the rook or pawn must do it.
notes.teaches: Trade the piece pressuring your centre to free your own hands — then the initiative is yours.
notes.plans: Exchange on f6, then attack unhindered.

notes.explains: The capture on f6 with check is the moment — it can't be delayed without losing d4, and the point of the earlier rook shift is that Black can no longer keep the kingside pawns intact. The structure shatters and the king is exposed.
notes.teaches: Time a structural-damage capture to the exact moment your centre still holds.
notes.plans: Break the kingside pawns, then attack the bare king.

notes.explains: Once more the Fantasy — the pawn to f3 keeps the centre. This game is the crash course in the big-centre structures it leads to.
notes.teaches: f3 defends the centre with a pawn and heads for a space-based middlegame.

notes.explains: After the knight to f6, the pawn to e5 kicks it and claims a broad centre. The knight has to scramble to d5 while White builds a spatial clamp with d4 and e5.
notes.teaches: When the centre is yours, hit the knight with e5 and seize the space.
notes.plans: Chase the knight, expand, and squeeze.

notes.explains: The pawn to c4 chases the knight again and grabs queenside space with tempo — White is simply taking the whole centre and more room, the Fantasy dream.
notes.teaches: Gain space with tempo by kicking the centralized knight.

notes.explains: With Black's knights parked on the queenside, White strikes with d5 in the centre, ripping open lines toward the kingside where the pieces are aimed.
notes.teaches: Break in the centre to open lines toward the wing where you are stronger.

notes.explains: The pawn to a6 questions the bishop at once. Unlike the Ruy Lopez there is no e5-pawn to defend, so the bishop has little reason to sit on b5 — it must either retreat or take.
notes.teaches: …a6 in the Rossolimo puts the question immediately — the bishop has no strong pawn target to justify staying.
notes.plans: Provoke the trade or the retreat, then develop.

notes.explains: After the capture on c6 the recapture with the b-pawn does double the pawns — but Black gets the bishop pair and a strong central pawn mass. Structure isn't everything; the two bishops and the half-open b-file are real compensation.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are fine when you get the bishop pair and central control in return.
notes.plans: Open the position for the two bishops and press the b-file.

notes.explains: The bishop to g4 pins the knight on f3 — but the real lesson is timing: when do you cash a pin, and when do you keep the tension?
notes.teaches: A pin is a resource to be timed, not a move to resolve automatically.

notes.explains: Facing White's flexible Bf4 system, Black commits to a King's Indian with d6 rather than the Grünfeld's d5. The lesson is transitions: read White's setup and choose the structure that punishes it.
notes.teaches: Stay flexible — pick your central structure, King's Indian or Grünfeld, based on how White develops.
notes.plans: Expand on the queenside with c6, a6 and b5.

notes.explains: Black expands on the queenside with a6 and b5, grabbing space and opening the bishop's diagonal. Against White's slow centre, the play belongs on the wing where Black is quicker.
notes.teaches: When White plays a slow central system, seize space on the queenside with a6 and b5.

notes.explains: The game transitions into a Benoni: after Black plays c5, White pushes d5, and Black gets the classic queenside majority with the long-diagonal bishop pointing straight through the position.
notes.teaches: These King's Indian setups can transition into a Benoni where Black plays on the queenside behind the fianchetto bishop.

notes.explains: The key: recapture the pawn with the knight, not the queen. Instead of exposing the queen, Black heads for a blockading knight on d5 — the dream piece against an isolated queen pawn.
notes.teaches: Against an IQP structure, a knight recapture aiming for the d5 blockade beats an early queen sortie.
notes.plans: Blockade d5, develop, and press the isolani.

notes.explains: The knight lands on d5 — the ideal blockading square. This is exactly the version the side facing an isolated queen pawn dreams of: the pawn on d4 is frozen and becomes a long-term target.
notes.teaches: A knight blockading on d5 both stops the IQP and radiates over the whole board.
notes.plans: Develop around the blockade and trade into a good endgame.

notes.explains: Develop the knight to c6, adding pressure to the d4-pawn. With the rock on d5 and pieces coming out with tempo, Black is very comfortable.
notes.teaches: Complete development while every piece leans on the isolated pawn.
notes.plans: Pile onto d4 and keep the blockade.

notes.explains: The pawn to e6 solidifies the blockade — it can transpose into well-known Caro-Kann middlegame theory, and in any case leaves Black with a pleasant, safe position.
notes.teaches: Cement the d5-blockade with e6 for a rock-solid structure.
notes.plans: Finish development behind the fixed d5 point.

notes.explains: The d5 break arrives anyway — the whole drawback of White's quiet Be2. The pawn strikes e4, and with our pieces already developed and active, Black equalizes on the spot.
notes.teaches: In the Accelerated Dragon, ...d5 is the freeing break White can only stop by putting the bishop on c4.

notes.explains: Knight takes c3 keeps the imbalance alive instead of drifting into a dead trade. From c3 it hits the queen on d1 and the bishop on e2 — however White recaptures, his pawn structure suffers.
notes.teaches: Prefer a move that damages the opponent's structure over a symmetrical simplification when you need winning chances.

notes.explains: The knight belongs on d2, not c3 — the whole point of the King's Indian Attack. On c3 it invites dxe4 and a queen trade that would kill the attack; on d2 White keeps the queens on and the plan intact.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian Attack, develop the knight to d2 to avoid a queen-trading dxe4 and keep attacking chances.
notes.plans: g3, Bg2, then e5 and a kingside attack.

notes.explains: The pawn to c3 after Nf3 and d6 is the Delayed Alapin — a relatively harmless anti-Sicilian, but genuinely dangerous against an unprepared opponent, aiming for a broad centre with d4.
notes.teaches: The Delayed Alapin is a low-theory system that punishes imprecise Sicilian play.
notes.plans: Prepare d4 and build the centre.

notes.explains: The little pawn to h3 restrains the light-squared bishop — and it screens a trap worth remembering: grabbing the e4-pawn with the knight loses a piece to a queen check on a4 and the follow-up on a5. It is very easy to forget.
notes.teaches: Before snatching e4 in these lines, check for the Qa4+/Qa5 fork that wins the loose knight.
notes.plans: Restrain the bishop, then take the centre.

notes.explains: The bishop to d3 is the Kopec-style idea — an odd-looking post until you see the plan: the bishop will reroute to c2 and support a central break, eyeing the kingside.
notes.teaches: A bishop on d3 headed for c2 backs up e4 and the coming d4 break.
notes.plans: Reroute to c2, play d4, and attack.

notes.explains: The bishop steps to c2, clearing the d-file and readying the d4 break while keeping the powerful diagonal aimed at Black's kingside.
notes.teaches: Clear the d-file for the central break while keeping the bishop's attacking diagonal.
notes.plans: Play d4 and expand.

notes.explains: The pawn to c4 is the Maróczy Bind — White grips d5 and e4 and plays for a slow squeeze. At club level it is far less scary than its reputation: it demands very precise positional play from White, and Black has a string of tricky responses.
notes.teaches: The Maróczy Bind is a positional clamp, not an attack — it punishes imprecise handling, not the defender.
notes.plans: Trade a pair of knights, keep the c6-pawn as a clamp of your own, and press the semi-open b-file.

notes.explains: The first trap begins here: capturing on c6 is the tempting error. Black recaptures and the queenside opens in Black's favour.
notes.teaches: In the Maróczy, an early capture on c6 concedes the b-file and hands Black the initiative.
notes.plans: Recapture toward the centre and watch for the e5 push.

notes.explains: And the follow-up e5 walks into it — a very tempting pawn thrust that simply loses.
notes.teaches: A tempting central push can hang to an in-between check — always look for the zwischenzug first.
notes.plans: Answer with the queen check on a5.

notes.explains: The point: the queen check on a5 wins the e5-pawn back with interest — never forget this resource. After the block, the pawn falls and Black is a healthy pawn up.
notes.teaches: The queen check on a5 is the standard refutation of White's e5 grab in this line.
notes.plans: Collect e5, then finish developing a clean pawn up.

notes.explains: The pawn to f3 is the Fantasy Variation — it props up e4 with a pawn instead of a piece, keeps the whole centre, and turns the Caro into a sharp, attacking fight.
notes.teaches: f3 defends the centre with a pawn so White can play for space and an attack, not a quiet game.
notes.plans: Hold the centre, aim the pieces at f7, and castle.

notes.explains: White gives up the bishop to crash into f7. The point sits behind it: once the king is dragged out to f7, the knight on f3 can leap away and unveil a check from the rook down the file — a discovered check that wins the material back with the king stranded.
notes.teaches: Sacrifice to strip the king when a discovered check waits behind the very piece you give up.

notes.explains: The knight lands on e6 with check and forks the king on f8 and the queen on d8 at once. The king must move, and the queen falls.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king and queen stand a knight's-move apart, the square that forks them wins the queen.

notes.explains: The bishop to c4 is an early, offbeat anti-Sicilian, aiming at f7 before developing the centre. The clean way to meet it is to blunt that bishop rather than fear it.
notes.teaches: Against an early Bc4, prepare to challenge it with …e6 and …d5 — bite on granite.
notes.plans: Play …e6, develop, and hit the bishop with …d5.

notes.explains: The pawn to e6 prepares the freeing …d5, walling off the c4-bishop's diagonal. There is no rush — the bishop isn't going anywhere, so develop first and break when ready.
notes.teaches: …e6 shuts the c4-bishop's diagonal and readies the …d5 central break.
notes.plans: Develop the knight, then strike with …d5.

notes.explains: Develop the knight to f6, adding a piece and pressure on e4 before committing the centre. With everything ready, …d5 will challenge White head-on.
notes.teaches: Complete development before the freeing break so it lands with full force.
notes.plans: Follow with …d5 and equalise comfortably.

notes.explains: The bishop check on b5 poses real problems at first — it forces a piece to appear on d7 and, in doing so, cuts the contact between Black's queen and the d5-pawn.
notes.teaches: A well-timed b5 check can sever the defence of a pawn by forcing an awkward block.
notes.plans: Exploit the loosened d5-pawn.

notes.explains: Rather than the loosening queen sortie to f3 — which Black meets with a6 — the sound choice is the pawn to d4, taking the centre and keeping every option open.
notes.teaches: Prefer a solid central move to a committal queen raid that invites a6 with tempo.
notes.plans: Build the centre, then decide on c4 once lines open.

notes.explains: This time not the Advance but the knight to d2 — the Tarrasch. It looks odd because it blocks in the c1-bishop, so the whole point had better be worth that.
notes.teaches: The Tarrasch develops the knight to d2, accepting a temporarily blocked bishop for other gains.
notes.plans: Nd2, then e5 and c3.

notes.explains: The pawn to e5 gains space and kicks the knight, which tucks back to d7. Now the clamp is up and White has the familiar French space advantage.
notes.teaches: e5 clamps the centre and drives the f6-knight to a passive square.
notes.plans: Advance e5, keep the space.

notes.explains: Here is why d2 was worth blocking the bishop: when Black hits with c5, White answers with the pawn to c3 and keeps the centre fully intact. It's the best of both worlds — pieces develop, the d4-e5 chain holds, and the other knight will take over guarding d4.
notes.teaches: Nd2 lets White meet ...c5 with c3, holding the centre while developing — the knight's payoff.
notes.plans: c3 to hold d4, develop behind it.

notes.explains: The knight to f3 — the g-knight, not the natural-looking knight to b3. For decades this was thought inferior because d4 is hard to hold, but engines flipped the verdict: it's the more testing move.
notes.teaches: Modern theory prefers Ngf3 over Nb3 despite the harder-to-defend d4-pawn.
notes.plans: Ngf3, castle, don't fear for d4.

notes.explains: And this is the modern question the computers asked: what if you simply don't defend d4 at all? Castle and let the pawn go — in return you get a lead in development, more space, and the e5-pawn clamping the centre.
notes.teaches: Sacrifice d4 for development, space, and the e5-clamp rather than passively defending it.
notes.plans: O-O; let d4 fall for the initiative.

notes.explains: This is the move that holds it all together — the knight to f3. After the queen grabs on d4 the bishop and pawns are hanging and the position would collapse without it, but the knight develops with tempo, driving the queen off before she can cash in. From here White must keep following up accurately, like in any d4-pawn gambit.
notes.teaches: Recapture the initiative with a developing move that hits the greedy queen with tempo.
notes.plans: Nf3, chase the queen, keep the lead.

notes.explains: The bishop to f4 outside the pawn chain is the London System — a solid, low-theory setup White can play on autopilot. Black should meet it with a clear, active plan rather than mirroring passively.
notes.teaches: The London is easy to play but not threatening — answer it with an active, concrete plan.
notes.plans: Build c5/Nc6 and pressure b2 with the queen.

notes.explains: Black sets up the standard counter: pawns on d5 and c5 with the knight on c6, striking at White's centre and preparing pressure on the queenside.
notes.teaches: Against the London, hit the centre with c5 and develop the knight to c6.
notes.plans: Prepare the queen sortie to b6.

notes.explains: The queen to b6 is the most standard way to play — it eyes the b2-pawn and the loose queenside, forcing White to react before he can complete his comfortable setup.
notes.teaches: Queen to b6 is the thematic London antidote — it targets b2 and asks White real questions.
notes.plans: Pressure b2 and c4-type breaks, seizing the initiative.

notes.explains: The principled reply is the pawn to d5, striking the centre at once — one of the two main lines, and the move that keeps Black fully in the game.
notes.teaches: Meet the Alapin with the central break d5 before White completes the big centre.
notes.plans: Trade in the centre and develop the queen actively.

notes.explains: The queen recaptures on d5 — centralised, but exposed. That early queen is the target White will develop against, gaining time with each piece that comes out.
notes.teaches: An early recapturing queen is active but vulnerable — its exposure hands the other side tempi.
notes.plans: Chase it with natural developing moves.

notes.explains: White answers with the pawn to d4 — the standard Alapin tabiya. From here Black chooses between the knights to c6 or f6, and the c-pawn tension defines the middlegame.
notes.teaches: The exd5 Qxd5 d4 structure is the Alapin main battleground — small centre versus the c-pawn tension.
notes.plans: Develop with tempo and keep the tension.

notes.explains: With the knight on c6 the tension between the c5- and c3-pawns sits unresolved — and usually Black should not release it, since capturing on d4 would open the c3-square for White's knight.
notes.teaches: Holding pawn tension is often better than releasing it into your opponent's development.
notes.plans: Keep the tension; develop and pressure the queen.

notes.explains: The knight to d2 accepts that Black may take on f3 and damage the structure — but the plan comes first: reroute the knights and hit the exposed queen. The structural cost is worth the initiative.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a slight structural concession is the price of a faster, more active plan.
notes.plans: Follow with the bishop to c4, gaining time on the queen.

notes.explains: The bishop to c4 strikes the queen, gaining a tempo and driving Black to react while White completes development and keeps the initiative.
notes.teaches: Develop with tempo against a centralised queen — every gained move compounds.
notes.plans: Chase the queen, castle, and press.

notes.explains: The bishop reaches g7 and leans down the long diagonal, pressing at once on the knight that anchors White's centre.
notes.teaches: The fianchettoed bishop is the Dragon's engine — it fights for the centre from the corner.
notes.plans: Castle, then break the centre.

notes.explains: The pawn to c3 is a mediocre choice: it props up the d4-knight and blunts the g7-bishop, but it develops nothing and, worse, robs White's own knight of its natural c3 square — so White's queenside comes out passively.
notes.teaches: A pawn move that solves one problem can create a bigger one — here c3 steals the best square from White's own knight.
notes.plans: Develop naturally and exploit White's slow queenside.

notes.explains: No need to reinvent anything: the knight comes to f6, then castling, then the pawn to d5 in one move. In the accelerated setup Black often never needs the small d6 step at all.
notes.teaches: The accelerated move order aims for the full central break in a single move — d5, not d6 then d5.
notes.plans: Knight to f6, castle, strike with d5.

notes.explains: The bishop to b5 simply drops the e4-pawn — there is nothing defending it, and the f6-knight is ready to collect.
notes.teaches: Before committing a piece, check what it stops defending — b5 abandons e4.
notes.plans: Take the free pawn.

notes.explains: The knight snaps off e4 — a clean extra pawn, and the whole setup already pays off.
notes.teaches: When a central pawn hangs for nothing, take it and ask questions later.
notes.plans: Consolidate the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Recapture toward the centre with the d-pawn: it opens the queen's file, frees the light-squared bishop onto a juicier diagonal, and leaves Black with the two bishops — a pawn up.
notes.teaches: Recapturing toward the centre trades a doubled pawn for open lines and the bishop pair — usually a fine deal.
notes.plans: Open the position for the two bishops.

notes.explains: The queen tucks onto c7 — a universal, safe post. The pawn on c6 already guards the b5 and d5 outposts, so the queen sits behind it untouchable while keeping the tension.
notes.teaches: Queen to c7 behind a c6-pawn is a standard, safe home across many Sicilians.
notes.plans: Keep the tension and prepare the central pawns.

notes.explains: The knight centralises on d5 — a magnificent outpost that also stops the freeing bishop to f4. From here the central pawns are ready to roll.
