notes.teaches: A knight on a protected central outpost is worth more than a pawn grab elsewhere — centralise and dominate.
notes.plans: Follow with the central pawn storm.

notes.explains: Time for the main plan: the pawn to e5 kicks the knight off d4, and f5 with e4 follows, ramming the pawns down the board. White's pieces are loose and hard to coordinate; Black's are anchored.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are better anchored, open with a pawn storm — push the loose enemy pieces around.
notes.plans: e5, then f5 and e4 — roll the centre.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to c4, aiming at f7 — the sharp Sozin-style setup. Black just keeps developing; depending on White's next move it will be castling, or d6, or sometimes d5 in one go.
notes.teaches: Against the aggressive bishop on c4, complete development and keep the central break flexible.
notes.plans: Castle, hold the d-pawn, and choose the break later.

notes.explains: Castling first, and deliberately NOT the pawn to d6 yet — holding it back preserves maximum flexibility. That reserve pays off if White castles, when the one-move d5 break becomes available.
notes.teaches: Delaying a committal pawn move keeps your best break in reserve.
notes.plans: Keep the d-pawn home until d5 in one move is on.

notes.explains: The knight retreat to e2 is a poor choice — it steps off the strong d4-square passively and hands Black an immediate way to challenge in the centre.
notes.teaches: A passive retreat that abandons a strong central post invites an immediate counter.
notes.plans: Hit back at once while White is disorganised.

notes.explains: The knight leaps to g4, harassing the e3-bishop — a move that can be genuinely nasty here, since the bishop has no comfortable square that keeps everything defended.
notes.teaches: With the queen still home, the g4-knight jab against the e3-bishop is a standard Dragon resource.
notes.plans: Follow up with the queen sortie to b6.

notes.explains: The queen swings to b6 — a garden-variety double attack, hitting the f2- and b2-pawns at once. It comes with risk, since the light-squared bishop is still at home, but the fork is real and White can only defend one pawn.
notes.teaches: A queen on b6 forking f2 and b2 is a classic Sicilian double attack — one pawn must fall.
notes.plans: Take the pawn White doesn't defend.

notes.explains: Grab it — the pawn on b2. The queen looks adventurous but it won't be trapped: the a3-square is a ready retreat and there are escape routes to spare, so this is simply a clean extra pawn.
notes.teaches: Before a deep pawn-grab, check the queen's escapes; with a3 available on b2 there is no trap.
notes.plans: Retreat to a3 and consolidate the extra pawn.

notes.explains: The knight comes back from its loose post on g4 to the fine central square e5, hitting the c4-bishop as it arrives — its job on g4 is done, and e5 is a much sturdier home.
notes.teaches: Reroute a knight that has done its job before it becomes a target — g4 to e5 with tempo.
notes.plans: Consolidate the centre, then untangle the queenside.

notes.explains: The pawn to g5 chases the bishop off the board's active diagonal altogether. Booting the strong piece unburdens the position and lets Black consolidate the extra material in peace.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are your only problem, push them back with pawns and consolidate.
notes.plans: Follow with d6 once the pressure eases.

notes.explains: Now the pawn to d6 is safe — e7 is well covered — so Black finally locks the centre without weakening the dark squares that a combined g6-and-e6 would have left soft.
notes.teaches: Choose d6 over e6 when you've already committed g6 — it keeps the dark squares intact.
notes.plans: Complete development and convert the extra pawn.

notes.explains: The knight to g4 with check is crushing — it drives the exposed king onto the run into a mating net, and Black's attack, a pawn up already, simply finishes the game.
notes.teaches: Once the enemy king is dragged into the open, forcing checks convert the attack.
notes.plans: Deliver the checks and mate.

notes.explains: The bishop to c4 looks, on the surface, like a positional mistake — it invites the knight to be hit — but it is a fresh, concrete idea: the bishop eyes f7 and d5, and the tactics justify it.
notes.teaches: A move that looks positionally wrong can be justified by concrete tactics — check before dismissing it.
notes.plans: Pressure f7 and the d5-knight with active piece play.

notes.explains: The knight develops to f6 before the d-pawn moves — the accelerated point. Holding the pawn home keeps the d5 break available in a single move, so the knight comes out first.
notes.teaches: Develop the knight before committing the d-pawn to preserve the one-move central break.
notes.plans: Castle, then strike with d5.

notes.explains: Castle first — the d5 break is only safe once the king is tucked away. Fire it too early and the capture on c6 followed by the bishop check on e6 forks the king and the rook.
notes.teaches: Sequence matters: castle before d5, or a bishop check on e6 forks king and rook.
notes.plans: King to safety, then break with d5.

notes.explains: The bishop to c4 sets the stage — a bishop aimed at f7 against a fianchettoed position is the precise precondition for the center fork trick.
notes.teaches: A bishop on c4 (or c5) facing a fianchetto is the trigger for the center fork trick.
notes.plans: Spring the trick with the knight capture on e4.

notes.explains: The center fork trick: the knight takes on e4. It looks like a blunder — the knight is simply captured — but the follow-up wins the piece straight back.
notes.teaches: The center fork trick sacrifices a knight on e4 to regain it by a re-forking pawn push.
notes.plans: Meet the recapture with d5.

notes.explains: There is the fork: the pawn to d5 hits the knight and the c4-bishop at once, and the piece comes back — the move that gives the trick its name. In this version White cannot even win the pawn back easily.
notes.teaches: The pawn to d5 re-forks the two pieces — the trick nets a clean pawn here.
notes.plans: Recapture toward the centre and keep the extra pawn.

notes.explains: After the capture on c6, recapture with the b-pawn — now the c6-pawn guards the d5-pawn, so the extra material holds even as the file opens. This is exactly where White pays for the wasted a3-move.
notes.teaches: Recapture toward the passed/attacked pawn so your own pawn defends it.
notes.plans: Convert the extra piece; open the b-file.

notes.explains: The knight has nowhere good: it can't return to c3 without being forked again on the fourth rank, and any other retreat drops the b2-pawn with tempo. White is simply lost.
notes.teaches: A well-placed pawn fork leaves the knight no safe square — every retreat costs material.
notes.plans: Collect the material and simplify.

notes.explains: Recapture on c4 — a clean pawn up — and note what is NOT played: taking b2 with the bishop. In the Accelerated Dragon you keep the fianchettoed bishop unless you truly must part with it.
notes.teaches: Guard your fianchettoed bishop; don't trade it off for a b2-pawn grab.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop, promote the extra pawn later.

notes.explains: Loose pieces drop off. The rooks are uncoordinated and the rook on b1 is undefended, so the bishop check on c3 ends it — the fork can't be answered without losing material.
notes.teaches: When the enemy rooks are uncoordinated, look for a forcing check that wins a loose piece.
notes.plans: Cash in and convert.

notes.explains: The bishop check on b5 forces a piece to d7 — by definition an awkward square that clogs Black's development and cuts the queen off from the d5-pawn.
notes.teaches: A check that forces a clumsy block on d7 wins a small, lasting positional edge.
notes.plans: Retreat the bishop and take the centre.

notes.explains: Retreat the bishop to e2 and, after the knight recaptures, grab the centre with the pawn to d4 — a nice, broad pawn centre with the better development.
notes.teaches: Decline the trade and claim the centre — the awkward d7-bishop lingers.
notes.plans: Build the centre and develop with a pull.

notes.explains: Black's knight to c6 here is a sloppy move: the minor pieces end up unsupported, with no pawns around them. The accurate order is e6 or c6 first, giving the pieces a foundation.
notes.teaches: Develop pieces onto squares your pawns support — knights without a pawn framework drift.
notes.plans: Exploit the loose pieces with central pressure.

notes.explains: After the queen recaptures, the pawn to d4 sets the standard structure. Knowing this move isn't enough — you have to know the follow-up, because Black's choices here decide the character of the game.
notes.teaches: Memorising a move is worthless without its plan — the follow-up is the real theory.
notes.plans: Develop with tempo and hold the centre.

notes.explains: Releasing the tension early with cxd4 is a risky inaccuracy: it sets White's d-pawn in motion as a strong central passer instead of leaving it under pressure. Conceptually, Black has done White a favour.
notes.teaches: Don't release central tension when it frees the opponent's pawn into a passer.
notes.plans: Use the mobile d-pawn as a spearhead.

notes.explains: The knight to c6 hits the d4-pawn, so White must defend it — the knight comes to f3, guarding the pawn and continuing development smoothly.
notes.teaches: Defend the central pawn with a developing move that also builds toward castling.
notes.plans: Support d4, complete development, and advance.

notes.explains: The bishop to b5 pins the knight on c6. In the Exchange Caro, White plays on the light squares, and pressuring or trading off that knight is the natural plan.
notes.teaches: In the Exchange, use the light-squared bishop to pin and challenge Black's active knight.
notes.plans: Trade toward a clean structure and press the small edge.

notes.explains: White takes on c6; the recapture will double Black's pawns, settling for a small but lasting structural edge — the Exchange's quiet way of pressing.
notes.teaches: Give up the bishop pair to saddle the opponent with doubled pawns and a fixed weakness.

notes.explains: The knight jumps to the c5 outpost, a strong square Black cannot easily challenge. If Black trades it off, recapturing only wrecks his pawns further.
notes.teaches: Plant a knight on an outpost the opponent is forced to react to.

notes.explains: This is the Rubinstein French — Black gives up the centre with the capture on e4 for a rock-solid, if slightly passive, structure. It can arrive through the Tarrasch or the Nc3 move order, and every e4-player has to know how to handle it.
notes.teaches: The Rubinstein trades central tension for solidity; recognise it from either move order.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, keep the space edge.

notes.explains: Trading on f6 reaches the main tabia of the line. From here White has five or six reasonable setups — g3, the classical Bd3 — but the one with the best modern reputation is coming.
notes.teaches: After the knight trade, this is the Rubinstein tabia where White chooses a setup.
notes.plans: Pick a setup and develop.

notes.explains: The move is the pawn to c3, and it's easy to misread as purely positional. Yes, it reinforces d4 — but it also opens the d1-a4 diagonal, and the check on a4 is a major resource in these positions as long as Black's king sits on e8.
notes.teaches: c3 both supports d4 and unveils Qa4+ ideas against the uncastled king.
notes.plans: c3, keep Qa4+ in the toolbox.

notes.explains: The bishop to e3 develops with a point — it leans on c5, and the real threat is simply to capture there. A developing move that also poses a concrete question is worth two.
notes.teaches: Develop with pressure: Be3 eyes c5 and threatens dxc5.
notes.plans: Be3, then dxc5.

notes.explains: Now the knight to e5 — the perfect moment to centralise it. The check on a4 would achieve nothing, since Black just plays the bishop to d7 and you've only helped him develop; the knight on e5 is the real prize.
notes.teaches: Don't play a check that develops the opponent; centralise where it actually improves your game.
notes.plans: Ne5, dominate the centre.

notes.explains: Leaning toward the capture on c5 — into an endgame rather than a middlegame. It's not clearly the best, but it poses Black an immediate dilemma: take on e3 and enter the ending, or not. Posing problems has value of its own.
notes.teaches: A slightly committal choice that forces the opponent to solve a problem can be practically strong.
notes.plans: dxc5, invite the ending.

notes.explains: Queens come off and the pawn recaptures on e3. Black has lost the right to castle, and while White's e-pawns are doubled, the c5-b4-c3 wall is about to strangle any queenside counterplay — an excellent structure to grind from.
notes.teaches: Trade into an ending where your structure denies the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Fix the queenside, improve every piece.

notes.explains: Start with the knight to c4 — the move you want anyway. It's flexible, it discourages the bishop coming to f6 because the knight to d6 arrives with tempo, and it keeps every option open.
notes.teaches: Play the move you'll want regardless first — it keeps flexibility and pre-empts the opponent's plan.
notes.plans: Nc4, discourage ...Bf6.

notes.explains: This c5-b4-c3 construction, which shows up from many openings, is superb at winding down all of Black's queenside counterplay. As long as that chain holds, Black simply can't get his pawns moving.
notes.teaches: A fixed c5-b4-c3 wall neutralises the opponent's pawn breaks — keep it intact.
notes.plans: Preserve the clamp, play on both wings.

notes.explains: The king walks to d2 to shepherd the c3-pawn — because you shouldn't tie a heavy piece to a menial defensive job. The rook on d8 isn't dangerous, and the king, the piece not yet participating, is the perfect defender; its home is c2.
notes.teaches: Defend a pawn with the least valuable idle piece; don't chain a rook to a menial task.
notes.plans: Kd2-c2 to hold c3.

notes.explains: Get the bishop out first with the move to e2, heading for f3. When Black tries the bishop to d7 and c6 for the long diagonal, White meets it on f3 — a defended square from which the bishop pressures b7.
notes.teaches: Route your bishop to a defended square that contests the opponent's best diagonal.
notes.plans: Be2-f3, pressure b7.

notes.explains: The pawn to a4, as planned — it prepares b5 and the advance of the queenside pawn majority. Meanwhile that light-squared bishop of Black's does nothing; judge a piece by what it actually achieves, not by how many squares it nominally covers.
notes.teaches: Evaluate a piece by its real function, not its square-count; advance your majority.
notes.plans: a4-b5, roll the majority.

notes.explains: The rook to d6 is a classic maneuver: place one heavy piece ahead on the file to clear the way for the other. And recapture on d6 with the knight, not the pawn — the pawn recapture hands Black a tempo, and keeping the current structure leaves his knight paralysed by the weak c3-pawn.
notes.teaches: Double on a file by stepping one piece ahead; recapture the way that preserves your winning structure.
notes.plans: Rd6, Rxd6 with the knight, then Rd1.

notes.explains: The pawn to h3 restricts Black's pawns and denies any ...g4 activity. There's no hurry — Black isn't threatening anything — so tighten the vice before converting.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, restrict the opponent's only source of activity before pushing for the win.
notes.plans: h3, deny counterplay.

notes.explains: Here's the tactic that wins a second pawn: the pawn to f4 knocks the bishop off e5, and after the trade White captures on f6 with check and comes around to collect on h5. It doesn't end there — the bishop will fight back to e5, and the knight is freed by walking the king to e4 to dislodge it.
notes.teaches: Break with a pawn to dislodge a blockader, then harvest weak pawns with checks and king marches.
notes.plans: f4, fxf6+, Nxh5, extract via Ke4.

notes.explains: Before the king commits to e4, fix the queenside with the pawn to c4. That's the magic of the line: after the king comes to e4 and Black tries the bishop to c3 to win the b4-linchpin of the majority, the knight jumps to f4 with check and escapes — c4 first is what makes it work.
notes.teaches: Fix a wing before advancing the king, so a saving in-between check extricates your piece.
notes.plans: c4, then Ke4 and Nf4+.

notes.explains: Now it's just too many passers. The pawn to c6 creates an outside passer on the a-file — the general rule is that a passed pawn wants to be as far from the enemy pieces as possible, and corner pawns are the hardest of all to stop.
notes.teaches: Make your passer as far from the enemy king as you can — outside and corner passers win.
notes.plans: c6, create the a-passer, promote.

notes.explains: White pushes the pawn to e5 — but this advance is premature. Unlike the French, where the same structure traps Black's light-squared bishop, here that bishop has not yet been shut in and can escape.
notes.teaches: The advance is only strong if it locks in the light-squared bishop — get the bishop out first and it loses its point.
notes.plans: Free the bishop before closing the position with e6.

notes.explains: The whole idea: develop the light-squared bishop to f5, OUTSIDE the pawn chain, before playing e6. The very piece that sits behind bars in the French is here a free, active bishop.
notes.teaches: In French-type structures, the problem child is the light-squared bishop — solve it first and the position is pleasant.
notes.plans: Then build the centre with e6 and c5.

notes.explains: And now the pawn strikes to c5 in a single move — no need for the Caro-Kann's slow c6-then-c5. The bishop is already free and the central break comes at once: the best of both worlds.
notes.teaches: Saving a tempo on the freeing break (c5 in one move) is a concrete gain over the Caro move order.
notes.plans: Pressure the d4-pawn and the centre.

notes.explains: The queen swings to b6, pressing on b2 and f2. If White grabs on c5, recapturing with the bishop hits f2 and the e5-pawn and breaks up White's pawn chain — so the pawn-grab only helps Black.
notes.teaches: A queen on b6 in these structures forks the weak b2/f2 pawns and dares the chain-breaking capture.
notes.plans: Provoke concessions on the queenside and against the chain.

notes.explains: The combination nets the pawn on a3, and the point is what comes next: the bishop returns to b4 with extremely awkward pressure, pinning and probing White's tangled queenside.
notes.teaches: Win the pawn AND keep the initiative — the bishop's return to b4 is the sting in the tail.
notes.plans: Keep the pieces active; convert the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Restraint: capturing on d4 here would be a blunder — after the recapture the queen delivers a nasty check and disrupts Black. There is no need to grab; simply develop the pieces.
notes.teaches: Don't snatch a pawn that hands the opponent a disruptive check — develop and keep the edge.
notes.plans: Complete development, then press the extra pawn.

notes.explains: The pawn to e6 is a common answer, contesting the centre directly and steering toward a French-flavoured structure.
notes.teaches: e6 meets the Alapin by fighting for the centre and preparing d5.
notes.plans: Choose between the Advance-French transposition and the traditional IQP line.

notes.explains: The traditional line: exchange in the centre so Black is left with an isolated queen pawn on d5. That lone pawn is the whole story of the middlegame — a strength in the attack, a weakness in the endgame.
notes.teaches: The Alapin can hand Black an isolated queen pawn — play against it long-term.
notes.plans: Blockade d5, trade pieces, and target the isolani.

notes.explains: Develop the knight to f3 and follow a simple rule of thumb: wait for Black to commit the dark-squared bishop, and only then capture on c5 — timing the trade so it damages Black's structure most.
notes.teaches: Against the IQP, time your captures to fix the weakness, don't rush them.
notes.plans: Blockade and pile onto d5.

notes.explains: The bishop check on b5 develops with tempo — and trades in general favour the side playing AGAINST the isolated pawn: the fewer pieces remain, the weaker that lone d5-pawn becomes.
notes.teaches: When you play against an IQP, welcome piece trades — they magnify the pawn's weakness.
notes.plans: Trade a pair, blockade, and squeeze the isolani.

notes.explains: With the setup complete, Black strikes the centre with e5 — the whole point of the knight on d7, challenging d4 head-on and claiming central space of Black's own.
notes.teaches: The Nbd7 setup exists to prepare the central e5 break.
notes.plans: Press d4 and e4; keep the tension.

notes.explains: After White clamps with e4, Black plays c6, patiently pressing the big white centre. White holds more space, but that centre is a long-term target Black keeps needling.
notes.teaches: Against a space advantage, apply steady pressure to the centre rather than forcing matters.

notes.explains: The queen to a5 is the point of this line — it leans on the knight on c3 and the whole centre, keeping pressure on while Black stays flexible.
notes.teaches: An active queen sortie to a5 pressures the c3-knight and White's centre at once.

notes.explains: White's quiet pawn to c3 keeps the cards hidden — it could become a London, a Torre, or a Colle. The right approach is to develop naturally and wait for White to commit before choosing a plan.
notes.teaches: Against a flexible, non-committal setup, develop soundly and react once it declares itself.
notes.plans: Fianchetto, castle, and wait to see White's system.

notes.explains: The bishop to g5 declares the Torre Attack — the pin alters the whole character of the game, pressuring the f6-knight and eyeing the dark squares around Black's king.
notes.teaches: Bg5 marks the Torre — the pin on f6 is the system's central idea.
notes.plans: Break the pin and challenge the bishop at the right moment.

notes.explains: Complete development by castling. Against the Torre there is no need to rush — finish the setup, then challenge the g5-bishop and strike in the centre on your own terms.
notes.teaches: Finish developing before confronting the pin — patience beats a premature challenge.
notes.plans: Castle, then question the bishop and expand.

notes.explains: The pawn to a6 reaches the Najdorf. When White answers with the early pawn to f3, that is the calling card of the English Attack — White braces the centre and plans to castle long and storm the kingside.
notes.teaches: An early f3 in the Najdorf signals the English Attack — brace, castle long, pawn-storm.
notes.plans: Meet the plan with central counterplay.

notes.explains: The pawn to e5 is the principled answer to the English Attack — it grabs central space and hits the d4-knight, forcing it back to b3 and blunting White's attacking build-up.
notes.teaches: Against the English Attack, …e5 gains the centre and kicks the knight before White gets rolling.
notes.plans: Follow with …Be6 and queenside play.

notes.explains: White grabs the centre with an early queen recapture on d4 — a kind of Center Game against the Sicilian. It is offbeat and, crucially, hands Black a lead in development by exposing the queen.
notes.teaches: An early queen recapture wins a pawn's worth of time back for the opponent — develop against it.
notes.plans: Hit the queen with tempo and develop fast.

notes.explains: The knight to c6 develops with tempo, attacking the exposed queen. This is the point: every move Black makes comes with a gain of time while White shuffles the queen.
notes.teaches: Chase a centralised queen with developing moves — the tempi are the compensation and more.
notes.plans: Develop, fianchetto, and seize the initiative.

notes.explains: The queen retreats, and Black already has a free, harmonious game — ready to fianchetto and castle with easy, active development while White has nothing to show for the early sortie.
notes.teaches: After chasing the queen home, convert the lead in development into lasting activity.
notes.plans: Fianchetto, castle, and press the centre.

notes.explains: The knight to f6 completes the Najdorf move order, and here is the great fork in the road: White must commit to a system — the aggressive Bg5, the English Attack, the quiet Classical, or the Bc4 lines — and only then does Black tailor the plan.
notes.teaches: The Najdorf hands White the first big decision — react to the system he chooses, don't pre-commit.
notes.plans: Choose …e5 or …e6 based on White's setup.

notes.explains: The bishop to d3 is a modern, dangerous try — but it leaves the knight on d4 loose, and that gives Black an immediate way to hit back while developing.
notes.teaches: When a setup leaves a central piece unsupported, strike at it at once.
notes.plans: Attack the d4-knight and develop with tempo.

notes.explains: The pawn to f3 is the Fantasy Variation — a bold way to prop up e4 with a pawn, keep the whole centre, and steer the Caro into a sharp, tactical fight.
notes.teaches: f3 defends the centre with a pawn so White can play for lines and an attack.
notes.plans: Hold the centre, develop, and open the kingside.

notes.explains: The pawn to a3 puts the question to the pinning bishop. It looks to just drop e4, but it is a deliberate gambit: take the knight and White collects the bishop pair and lasting dark-square targets.
notes.teaches: a3 offers e4 as a gambit for the two bishops and the holes Black's dark-squared bishop leaves behind.
notes.plans: Invite the capture on c3, then work the dark squares.

notes.explains: Black snatches on e4 again, but the raid is dubious. The knight grab on c3 is no real threat: the queen would step to d2, pinning that knight against the loose queen on a5 and simply winning it.
notes.teaches: Before fearing a fork on c3, spot the pin — Qd2 skewers the knight to the undefended queen on a5.

notes.explains: The queen swings via f3 to g3 — the ideal attacking post in the Fantasy. It steps out of the rook's way, trains straight down at the g7-pawn, and forces Black to weaken.
notes.teaches: g3 is the Fantasy queen's home — it clears the rook's file and bears on g7.
notes.plans: Threaten g7 and provoke a concession.

notes.explains: White takes on g7. It hands Black the open g-file, but it is a clean extra pawn, and White is betting the counterattack on g2 is a bluff.
notes.teaches: Grab the pawn when you can't refute your own attack — trust the material if the counter falls short.
